speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday while the Leader of the New Democratic Party was speaking to the second reading of this bill he said it was a veritable nightmare from an administrative point of view. I should like to spend a little time today documenting the statement made yesterday by my leader. In the remarks I made yesterday afternoon, I hope I made clear that this administrative nightmare is really inherent in the deficiencies of principle in the bill which are pointed out by the amendment under consideration at the present time.
I suggest very few Canadian people have any real inkling of just what lies before them if and when this bill becomes law. Not all people in Canada will read Hansard, but more people will read it than will read the fine print in the bill that is before us for consideration. I intend to spend part of my time in documenting this statement about an administrative nightmare by indicating through some actual references to the text of the bill just what form the nightmare may take. I suggest that if one considers the high number of applicants there have been for unemployment insurance this past winter, and the administrative nightmare that resulted from the operation of that act, one realizes that that was a very mild foretaste of what lies ahead for a great many Canadians if this bill is passed. Indeed, in my view, the two are interrelated.
I would like to suggest also that while my main concern is for the general citizenry of Canadaj I do have some feeling for the employees of the government of Canada who, if this bill becomes operative, will have the responsibility of trying to deal with irate and perplexed citizens. In fact, I would go so far as to suggest that what we should be considering, if we are going to pass this kind of bill, is the doubling or tripling of the number of members in this House, because if many of us had to spend a good deal of our time during this past winter trying to unravel some of the difficulties caused by the new unemployment insurance plan, we can be sure that sort of activity on our part will be trebled under this plan.
I suppose one should start with the clause which determines the amount of benefit paid under the bill. I suppose this might be described as the simplest part. It reads:
The amount of a benefit in respect of a child for any month in a benefit year is,

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
(a)	in the case of a child who is less than twelve years of age, $15, and
(b)	in the case of a child who is twelve or more years of age but less than eighteen years of age, $20, minus 33 cents for each full $100 of income by which the income of that child's family for the base calendar year exceeds
(c)	$4,500 when that child is the only child in the family,
I suppose it is fair to say that that involves a calculation which is relatively simple, so that part of the bill may be comprehensible to large numbers of people. However, the calculations involved become increasingly complicated as one starts deducting 33 cents for each additional full $100 of income. If a person has an income of $4,599.99, and a child who is 11 years old, that child will get $15; but if the income is $4,600, he would only get $14.67. That is perhaps the simplest part of the bill.
However, we then come to the part which is headed "Statement of Estimate of Income". Here we see a close relationship to the kind of calculation that is required of people who apply for the guaranteed income supplement. This section of the bill provides for the filing of a statement of income, otherwise the benefit cannot be approved. There have been complications in the dealings that people in receipt of the guaranteed income supplement have had with the government. Many members are fully aware of the difficulties connected with the adjustment of income and the reclaiming of benefits paid. Those are problems which come to the attention of members and problems with which the administrative officials have to deal. But let us remember that when we are speaking of people who are getting the guaranteed income supplement, by and large we are speaking of people who are receiving retirement benefits or who are in receipt of the basic old age security pension. These considerations do not apply when we are talking about benefits payable to or on behalf of children of parents who are earning an income.
In documenting what I consider to be a complete administrative nightmare, I should like to refer to those parts of the bill that deal with occasions when a family's income is reduced or increased, just to give some idea of the kind of gobbledygook with which an individual citizen is faced.. Let me make reference to that part of the bill which reads:
(2)	Where at any time during the base calendar year or during the fourth month of a current benefit year a parent
(a)	ceases to hold an office or employment previously held by him or ceases to carry on a business previously carried on by him, or
(b)	for any other reason suffers a loss or reduction of income, as a result of which event or occurrence it is reasonable to expect that the income of the family for the calendar year next following the calendar year in which the event or occurrence took place will be substantially reduced, the parents may, in such manner and within such time as are prescribed, file a statement of the estimated income of the family for that next following calendar year, in which case the income of the family for that calendar year shall be deemed to be the income of the family for the base calendar year.
(3)	Where at any time during the first eleven months of a benefit year, other than the fourth month, or during the eight-month period next before that benefit year a parent

(a)	ceases to hold an office or employment previously held by him or ceases to carry on a business previously carried on by him, or
(b)	for any other reason suffers a loss or reduction of income
as a result of which event or occurrence it is reasonable to expect that the income for the family for the calendar year in which the event or occurrence took place or for the next following calendar year will be substantially reduced, the parents may, in such manner and within such time as are prescribed, file a statement of the estimated income of the family for the calendar year in which the event or occurrence took place, in which case the income of the family received during that part of the calendar year after the month in which the event or occurrence took place divided by the number of months in that part of that calendar year and multiplied by twelve shall be deemed to be the income of the family for the base calendar year.
Then the bill repeats that exercise in semantics in dealing with the situation when the family income is increased. If anything is going to cause confusion and misunderstanding, is going to leave people not knowing where they stand from one month to the next in relation to the receipt of family allowance benefits, I suggest it is that formula set out in the bill. If one puts that provision together with the new and much more complex provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the result will be that each time somebody files a claim for unemployment insurance benefit he will probably have to file a statement showing what adjustment should be made in the family allowance payments to his children.
I notice that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Perrault) is in the chamber. I know he is well aware of some of the complexities faced by people who made application for unemployment insurance benefits last winter. I ask him to visualize the situation, if he continues to hold that office next winter, when people will not only be in turmoil over whether they get their unemployment insurance or not, but will be in turmoil over whether their family allowance cheques are to be cut off, increased or reduced.
People will be in a turmoil over what to do if they are laid off and their family income is reduced. They will need to know what to do if they are called back to work. I can just imagine what will happen in the case of some of the loggers on Vancouver Island who have been having problems with unemployment insurance. I can just imagine what will happen when they are called back to work again and their income is increased. They will have to go all through this exercise again. They will feel apprehension about their family allowance cheques in addition to worrying about whether their unemployment insurance cheques will catch up with them after they return to work. When the leader of my party suggested that this bill would lead to an administrative nightmare he was not exaggerating the impact of the bill.
In other parts of the bill, there are provisions to extract information respecting claimants from other departments of government. We have had a tradition in Canada that our incomes are known only to the Department of

National Revenue. Now, the Department of National Health and Welfare will have access to income information. In addition to that, income information may be given to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, the Department of Supply and Services, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and to an officer employed in Statistics Canada.

I hesitate to use this word, Mr. Speaker, but to check on this information we will create, under the terms of the bill, what can only be described as a government Gestapo service. If somebody makes a mistake in supplying income information, and somebody also takes the notion that he made the mistake knowingly, that person is liable to imprisonment. According to the terms of the bill:
Every person who knowingly makes a false or misleading statement in any application or statement required or permitted by this Act or makes any such application or statement that by reason of any non-disclosure of facts is false or misleading,
provides any person employed in the administration or enforcement of this Act or appointed to make an inquiry under this Act with any statement or information that is false in any material part-
The clause then refers to cashing cheques, and so on.
-is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars or to both.
Parents who make application under this legislation and who make a mistake in their applications, are liable to imprisonment for six months and fines of up to $1,000 if someone believes they made such mistake knowingly.
We have come to accept the fact that the Department of National Revenue is the body which polices our income returns to determine the accuracy of them. This may be necessary in order to ensure that all people carry their fair share of the tax burden. But if one starts multiplying that kind of authority and extending it to other government departments, then the ordinary citizen will feel so overwhelmed by this supervision of every move he makes, each time he is laid off, each time he goes back to work for a week or a month, and makes some mistake in reporting his income, that the scientists of Canada should be put to work developing a portable computer for all citizens which could be supplied with the family allowance cheques to help him avoid running afoul of the law. These illustrations support the statement made yesterday by the leader of the New Democratic Party when he moved the amendment opposing the principle of this bill, and suggested that the citizens of Canada had an administrative nightmare ahead of them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly my duty to speak to the motion for second reading of Bill C-170, to provide for the payment of benefits in respect of children.
Family Income Security Plan
This legislation, sponsored by the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) will turn into a nightmare for Canadian families, instead of an assistance measure. The government, I suggest, seeks by this legislation to replace the present family allowance plan which, as is generally known, is a universal plan applying to all children-those under 10 now receive $6 a month, those between 10 and 16 receive $8.
The bill before us purports to abolish the principle of universality instead of merely increasing family allowances. The government, on the one hand, will grant a very slight increase of these family allowances, giving $15 to children under 12, and $20 to children between 12 and 18.
On the other hand, however, while giving this slightly increased amount, the government will be establishing a nightmarish system for families which will end up by disgusting them rather than helping them.
As some hon. members have done before me, I will refer to certain clauses of the bill in order to clarify this point. In the government bill now before us, and according to paragraphs (a) (b) and (c) of subclause 1 of clause 6, a ceiling has been set on family income which, if exceeded, will entail a decrease in family allowances in respect of children and, under some circumstances, their eventual disappearance.
This bill provides that benefits of $15 and $20 will be reduced by 33 cents for each full $100 of excess family income. And as I said a few moments ago, Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to read these figures.
My colleagues of the Social Credit party and myself have made some calculations in this respect to see where we were heading.
For example, if the parents of an only child earn a yearly income of $6,000, the maximum allowable income of those parents will be deducted from this amount thus making a difference of $1,500 resulting in an allowance decrease of $4.95. The benefit in respect of the child will therefore amount to $15 less $4.95, or $10.05.
If the parents have two children, the income ceiling, according to the provisions of the bill, is set at $4,500 plus $500, making a total of $5,000. This amount is deducted from the gross income of $6,000, leaving an excess of $1,000 entailing a reduction of 10 times 33 cents, or $3.30. A child will be entitled in this particular case to $11.70.
This is all very intricate, Mr. Speaker. This is the system which is being foisted on every Canadian family.
For a couple with one child and an income of $8,000, the ceiling is set at $4,500 and the benefit at $11.55. For a family with two children and a gross income of $10,000, the ceiling would therefore be $5,500 and the benefit would decrease by $18.15. Thus we have the picture. And the bill says that the child will not even get 15 cents a month when the allowance is less than $5.
Such a bill has been introduced by the government, Mr. Speaker. How will it be enforced? In the recom-

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
mendation that goes with the bill it is said that this measure tends not only to provide for the benefits but also to provide for the calculation of such benefits and the determination of the persons or institutions to whom they are payable and the times at which they are payable.
That is very precise, Mr. Speaker. This means that in this measure the government provides for a whole administrative and technical system of red tape to get people into line, to determine whether the children of a given family will receive benefits or not.
To do that, through this legislation, the government provides for a selective approach. Instead of sending family allowances to all children, on a universal basis, as it is doing now, the government removes this principle, which has been taken for granted, and wants to adopt the selective approach. In other words, we are going to give allowances to certain children, on the basis of extraordinary complex calculations to which I referred a While ago.
How will such data be used to determine whether a family is to be assisted or not? A host of civil servants will make the decisions on the basis of increases or decreases in the number of children in each family, as well as on the basis of increases or decreases in family income. This is precisely the point on which I should like to elaborate.
In clause 8, for instance, we read that a statement of income must be submitted with the application. This means that if a family wants to receive family allowances, it will not get them until it has submitted a statement of income each year, somewhat in the same way as for an income tax return.
This legislation also provides that whenever some change occurs in the family income-be it the father's or the mother's-the family has to make a new statement of income. This, according to a very serious study made by technocrats, will have the effect of reducing the amount of allowances by 5, 10, 15 cents, $1, or more.
And if for some reason or other a person goes on strike or becomes ill, which would bring a change in his income, he must, in order to avoid making a false statement, being sued and having to pay a fine, make a statement to inform the government of the new circumstances.
I want to say straight out that I am going to oppose categorically the principle of this legislation which is only going to increase bureaucracy in Canada and to create more annoyances for Canadians. In short, this legislation, far from serving the population, will just increase its problems.
Mr. Speaker, needy families in Canada are already bothered no end because of all the welfare measures- both provincial and federal. A number of investigators go from home to home asking: Do you have any money in the bank? Do you have any money hidden in the house? Have you bought a new fridge or stove lately? Do you have any lodgers here, and, if so, how much

money do you get from them, and how long have they been staying here?
Such investigations are being made constantly, and people are being bothered by governments which spend most of their revenues on paying bureaucrats, instead of giving the money to families who need it.
The Unemployment Insurance Act is another measure enacted by the government to help families. It is good in itself, since it provides a worker who is temporarily unemployed with up to $100 per week in benefits. But in order to get it, he must deal with a whole army of bureaucrats, which is a terrible headache, no matter what the minister may say, regardless of the numerous delays. Why? Because the administration has been centralized and the number of officials unduly increased.
I shall give only one example to make the minister responsible for this bill realize what is involved here. There is a provision in this new Unemployment Insurance Act under which illness is covered, provided the patient submits a medical certificate.
But there is nothing in the act about the part to be played by the physician. In fact, the worker who becomes unemployed due to illness has to wait in line to obtain a medical certificate, and until he submits it, he is not entitled to any benefits.
And when he finally gets to see the doctor and to take up his time with that request, the latter issues a certificate between two appointments and sends it to the regional office. The public servant is then entitled, under the law, to decide whether this is a serious illness or not. The public servant reaches that decision on his own. I wonder what sort of ability he has to diagnose people's illnesses. He decides that that person will not be eligible to unemployment insurance benefits because his medical statement is incomplete or inaccurate. The claimant then gets the following answer: You are not eligible, for your medical certificate is incomplete. Therefore he must go through the whole process again, aware that the end result might be the same as the first time.
This shows how ridiculous the unemployment insurance legislation is. Indeed, the government is giving some public servants, who hardly know how to add or to sub-stract, the authority to decide whether people are ill or not. Finally, this legislation is more of a nuisance than anything else.
Now, what are we doing, at this time, with family allowances? Exactly the same thing. But there, the intrusion into people's privacy is even more obvious.
Instead of quite simply giving everyone, with a minimum of bureaucracy, the same right to receive allowances, the government prefers to "divide" the population into two segments, stating that those whose incomes are above $8,000 will no longer receive these allowances and those whose incomes are below $8,000 will be entitled to them, providing they report their income and
April 20, 1972

what they expect to receive during the year and advise the government of any change in their income, failing which their allowances will be discontinued.
What will happen, Mr. Speaker? It is quite simple. Mr. X's family, living on Y street in Victoriaville, will apply for family allowances. Mr. X will produce a statement of income which will be sent to a public servant. The public servant will compare the statement with the same family's income tax return, checking for possible false statements, and then if all these requirements have been met, and all the complicated calculations mentioned at the very start of my remarks have been carried out, the civil servant may send the family allowance right away. If he finds any details lacking, what will he do? He will say the decision on your family allowance will remain pending unless you supply such and such data, tell us for whom you worked, at what date, how much you earned, whether another member of your family besides yourself is working, etc., etc. The report will then come back to the civil servant who will work out the calculations and it will be months before the individual receives anything.
Mr. Speaker, it might be said: Yes, but there will be retroactivity. But what is the philosophy behind the government's introduction of legislation which, instead of just assisting the people, will strictly contribute to aggravate them? Here is an example of the ridiculous nature of the legislation. In case of a decrease in income, the family will have to file a statement with the government, otherwise the statement will automatically be false, and the family will probably be liable to a fine. These civil servants are experts on fines. What should the family do if the family income is reduced? Here is what the bill says at page 8:
(2) Where at any time during the base calendar year-
This means that the family will have to file a statement five, four, three, ten or twelve times a year, or as often as there is a change in the family income.
I resume the quotation:
Where at any time during the base calendar year or during the fourth month of a current benefit year, a parent
(a)	ceases to hold an office or employment previously held by him or ceases to carry on a business previously carried on by him, or
(b)	for any other reason suffers a loss or reduction of income,
Whatever this reduction of income may be.
I continue the quotation:
as a result of which event or occurrence it is reasonable to expect that the income of the family for the calendar year next following the calendar year in which the event or occurrence took place will be substantially reduced, the parents may, in such manner and within such time as are prescribed file a statement of the estimated income of the family for that next following calendar year;
There again, Mr. Speaker, what bureaucratic nonsen; Obviously, the family cannot estimate to the last ce the income it will be getting. Therefore, a statement an estimated income will have to be filed. If this fami makes a mistake, if it cannot anticipate everything will be accused of making a false statement, and c'o sequently will have to pay a fine.
Family Income Security Plan
I continue the quotation:
-in which case the income of the family for that calendar year shall be deemed to be the income of the family for the base calendar year.
And so on.
Subsection (4) provides the following:
-that the income of the family-will be substantially increased-
Then, line 39 reads as follows:
-file a statement of the estimated income of the family for the next following calendar year-
And so on, and so forth.
Mr. Speaker, to my mind, this bill is absolutely revolting. It will only add to the dissatisfaction amongst the people, the division between them. For instance, a family with one or two children receives $30 a month, the neighbour will ask how much they get in family allowances? He will be told $30. He can then obviously know exactly what the income of that family is because the same calculation will apply in all cases.
Before, a person's or a family's income was a personal thing which did not concern the whole town or country. Now, because of the system, the government will help to spread that much more dissension among people. That is exactly what the government seems to be looking for. Before, filling out your income tax form was relatively simple. With the tax reform, it has become so complicated a procedure that people must go to an accountant and pay his fee. Now, we will have to make a statement on income with regard to family allowances every time the financial situation changes. Is there anything more ridiculous, more revolting?
I shall give you an example to show what thinking lies behind this, the thinking that inspires the government. When a man becomes entitled to the old age security pension and his income is not adequate, he applies for the guaranteed income supplement. What is such person to do? Another income statement with a check of bank accounts, etc.
Mr. Speaker, why continue to bother the people, to socialize the individual, to control strictly all his activities? Why continue to do so and act in such a way that Canadians are increasingly becoming mere numbers in their country instead of builders? This is the aim of this government. On the contrary, the members of the Social Credit of Canada suggest that we stop bothering the people.
What will be the administrative costs of the family allowances program? It will cost millions of dollars merely for comptrollers, scientists, technocrats, investigators, etc. The remnants or the remainder will be paid as family allowances.
Mr. Speaker, why not establish a realistic social security system in Canada instead of being always negative, always bothering people, always making them dance a few steps before giving them a penny, doling out 42 cents a month in assistance as was the case with the old age

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
pension? Let us stop this tomfoolery if we are really serious in this House and start a social security program tailored to the needs of the individual. Let us give every Canadian family and every Canadian citizen the possibility of living decently in this country instead of constantly pestering them and giving them nothing but the crumbs left over once the bureaucrats have helped themselves.
Mr. Speaker, if we are intelligent enough to land on the moon, if we are clever enough to ensure that technology and progress keep on growing in Canada, we should be at least brilliant enough to create a financial system that will provide positive social security for Canadians.
I am aware, Mr. Speaker, that they will find it odd, in this House, that social credit is again referred to concerning this bill, but nevertheless this bill is in complete contradiction with the creditiste philosophy advocating for all a guaranteed minimum income so that they may live decently, an income paid automatically without any difficulty and investigation so that they may then keep on improving their lot without stumbling over officials.
I shall give you but one example. You will say: Yes, but this is expensive. But it does not cost more, on the contrary. If administration costs are reduced, there will be more money to give to people and less to bureaucrats.
Mr. Speaker, some of our colleagues say that the situation is not rosy out west. Why? Because the people from that area have too much wheat, too much of everything.
In Quebec things are going bad because there is too much wood, too much milk, in short too much of everything.
In the Maritim.es conditions are also bad because there is too much of everything. So, the government clamps down on production.
At the same time, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) grants millions of dollars to create employment and boost production. One man says produce more, the other argues against higher production.
I am thinking about the Canadian policy on milk, wheat, fisheries, etc.
The problem in Canada is that we have a sector called the production sector of which the Canadian people should be proud. Instead, three families out of five in Canada are literally starving. The Croll report on poverty changes nothing to the fact that we have over a million unemployed. Indeed, unemployment and welfare have become our main industries in Canada. We let people live in poverty, despite the high volume of production. This is a scandal in Canada: riches and poverty live side by side. And in order to solve the problem of minimum security, the government contrives all sorts of civil service gimmicks to go on irking people who, while they get entangled in all those investigations, will go on starving in their own country.
Yet Canada is the second largest country in the world. It is situated between two oceans and draws its wealth

from unlimited sources, but there is poverty nevertheless. But at the same time Denmark, a small country which can rely only on its mineral resources, enjoys a standard of living comparable with ours.
Japan, which has 122 million inhabitants living on twelve small islands, now ranks third among trading countries in the world. As for us, with a lot of mineral resources and an overflow in every field-minerals, wood products and all kinds of other resources-we give away our hardwood by granting timber concessions without doing anything to ensure forestation. As for softwood, we have so much that our factories, like Domtar, in Trois-Rivieres, must close down and dismiss their employees because they cannot transform all the wood. It is the same picture in fisheries.
In this country which is overflowing with wealth, there are people dying of starvation. This administration insists that there must be no inflation, that inflation is at the root of all our problems. Can anyone imagine such inconsistencies!
So, for the past three or four years, this administration fought mercilessly against inflation. To end up with what? Unemployment. And now that we are fighting this new enemy, prices are going up again. This is complete chaos.
And this bill has been given the same slant as those on unemployment insurance, social welfare and all the other plans which this government has introduced and which contributed directly to the growth of bureaucracy and the reduction of the real assistance which families need.
Mr. Speaker, since when does a Canadian government have the power to decide who has the right to live to discriminate between the children of families whose, income is $8,000 per year or less and those which earn in excess of $8,000? On whose authority does it exercise the power of deciding someone's fate while subordinating this right to the hypothetical results of various inquiries?
Hon. members realize that the control of the situation has shifted from the government to an all powerful bureaucracy that gobbles up millions of dollars collected through taxation to administer programs, while the Canadian people are only given bits and pieces.
I would be most interested to know what Canadians had to pay to officials to enable them to increase senior citizens' pensions by 42 cents a month and I would be greatly indebted to the minister who fights for this bill as if it were the apple of his eyes if he could tell us the estimated costs earmarked for the administration of the family allowance plan.
I would like to know what benefits will acrrue to the Canadian people and what will be the administrative costs of this program. But I am sure the hon. minister does not know the answer, because he does not care. He does not care to know how much the bill will cost. What matters is to shore up his control over each Canadian citizen, to increase the rub-a-dub for the Canadian people instead of helping them.
April 20, 1972

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people of Lotbiniere are thirsting for economic security and freedom. They do not want to be bothered any more. On the contrary, they want to be helped and encouraged to progress in life instead of being discouraged.
Did you ever notice that whenever someone is trying to make headway in Canada there is a government to hamper his efforts?
In the House, I have previously brought forward this fact. If the father of a family is working hard to get a decent income and succeeds in earning over $8,000, he will automatically lose his family allowances. Is it the way a hard-working man is being rewarded for his efforts? This is certainly not the proper way to encourage Canadians to have the interest of their country at heart.
Let us take the case of a student. He does not work during summer but, on the other hand, he will be granted the maximum grant available when he returns to school.
On the other hand, if he worked all summer, he will not be entitled to any bursaries from either government, federal or provincial. As a matter of fact, he will be told: "Considering your earnings of last summer, we cannot grant you a bursary. Therefore, the student who had nothing to do all summer long will get a bursary whereas the one who worked will not get anything. This is surely not a way to encourage people to help build their own country.
What afflicts me is that in spite of past experiences, in spite of the noisy display thrusted upon this House by the government, this same government is still following the way of control, which amounts to dominating the individual and assigning him "ceilings". The work and energies of the individual are subject to a never-ending control.
The same may be said of the farmers. Whenever one of them exceeds his milk quota,, not only is he deprived of any encouragement on the part of the government, but he also has to pay a tax, or a fine for having worked too hard. That is most economical!
Mr. Chairman, conditions have become unbearable. Our economy will never progress if it feeds only on the eloquence of our ministers. The Canadian economy will never work that way. Indeed, it will only work inasmuch as Canadians will play the game, inasmuch as the government will stop pestering them. Instead, let us give them whatever encouragement we can so they may co-operate in the building of a nation of their own.
Mr. Speaker, there is no other way. We must stop- and that is urgent-passing legislation that will merely help divide our people, to emphasize class struggles and discourage the individual.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to have to tell the House such things. I am really sorry to see the Canadian people in their present situation, due mainly to their having a majority government. The government claimed that with a majority, it could settle all problems, that a majority government was absolutely necessary to prevent disorder in Canada, to build up a sound economy and check unemployment.
Family Income Security Plan
Mr. Speaker, we have a majority government. What is it doing? It introduces measures designed to discourage initiative. More and more I have the impression that there are fewer and fewer people working in Canada and that it is the working people who provide for the increasing number of those who remain idle.

speechtext: No, this is not true!

speechtext:
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion says it is not true.
Mr. Speaker, I invite him to visit my riding again, where he is always welcome, and not to keep to Liberal circles. Then, I will introduce him to the people of Lotbiniere and he will find out that I am telling the truth.
On my street, Mr. Speaker, a father of eight children is working 14 or 15 hours a day. Because of that, he will be deprived of his family allowances, since he is earning over $8,000 a year. His neighbour, another man with a family, is on welfare and can support three children. That one will get the maximum allowance.
Perhaps the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion will tell me that this is all normal. As for me, I would tell him that I find it awkward to tell a worker to keep on working with all his heart, his energy, his life and his health and that whever he will earn over the ceiling will be given to someone else!
Mr. Speaker, I maintain that Canadians are entitled to live in their country and unless this government recognizes the right of Canadians to build their country, disagreement, the current conflicts in Quebec, social troubles which hurt us so much, and economic slowdown will prevail. This is due to the fact that everybody's problem is a money problem, and not a constitutional problem; it is not a problem of language, economic expansion or regional differences. We have reached the point where the whole country should be considered a designated area.
Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude by saying that the government has a choice to make and that it should make it now because the people are going to make it soon. Either we go on adopting gimmicks such as the one before us today, which only serves the purpose of irking the people and increasing the powers of technocrats, or in other words we go on treading the way of extreme socialism, or else we change our course and deal with the true problem in Canada, which is financial in character, we give each human person his freedom and security. and we recognize the right of each human being to life and security.
Mr. Speaker, I often ask two questions to which I have never been able to get an answer. Perhaps the minister could tell me how it is that we make reforms in all fields-it would take me longer than this day to list them all-except in the one monetary field.
I ask the minister why we can discuss any matter, except something which is taken in the House, the banking or financial reform. This golden calf is so sacred that we must hide to speak about it.

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
Mr. Speaker, the minister tells me that it is normal, because everything is okay. I strongly urge him to come and explain that to the Canadian people. It is urgent!
Reforms have been made in every field, except in the monetary field. When we refer to family allowances, etc. we hear not a word. All's well. When we mention the constitution, we hear not a word. All's well. When we refer to languages, we hear not a word. All's well. Discussions are sometimes held between Ottawa and the provinces, but they always boil down to the same problem, to wit who is going to tax: Ottawa or the provinces. Finally, everybody is speaking about financial matters, but instead of dealing with the monetary problem, the debate is carried on.
Mr. Speaker if the minister prefers to keep with those people who talk, good for him. As for me I would rather be with those who do things.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the speech we have just heard, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words in defence of this bill. The measure now before parliament proposes a new family income security plan which will directly benefit two and a half million Canadian families. One half of those families, that is, 1,250,000 Canadian families, will receive the maximum benefit under this plan, which is $15 per month per child under the age of 12 and $20 per month per child between the ages of 12 and 17. And these are non-taxable benefits.
The effect of this plan is to redistribute income, to place additional buying power in the hands of those who need it most. That is the basic principle of the bill and it is one which must be emphasized in the course of this debate. Although it is almost impossible to define in an objective way exactly what is meant by social justice, I am satisfied that the plan before us at least approaches such an ideal. It is true there are those who will cease to receive the family and youth allowances. But a wiser man than I once pointed out that social justice is not a single and simple ideal of society but that it is an essential part of a great complex of social change, and that to achieve it some things may have to be sacrificed. In this case, those with greater earning power in our society will have to sacrifice the monetary pittance which they now receive from the family and youth allowance plan.
No one pretends that the new family income security plan will of itself eradicate poverty within our borders. But it is an essential part of an evolving federal program designed to bring about total income security. It coordinates with the old age security plan, the guaranteed income supplement, the Canada Pension Plan, unemploy-1-ment insurance and the Canada Assistance Plan, all of which are designed to help ensure that needy families keep a roof over their heads, bread on the table-with perhaps some meat as well-and the bill collector away from the door.
It may be that those who succeed us in this chamber in years to come, will regard these various plans and

programs as merely timid steps toward a full scale guaranteed annual income. Such a massive extension and intensification of social justice as this may well be enacted in due course along with an amendment to the Bill of Rights stating that all Canadians have a democratic right to consume at least a basic minimum of the goods and services produced by a high-geared technological society such as our own.
Some Canadians, including some members of this House, have expressed concern about the complexity of the family income security plan, despite assurances as to the efficiency of operation of this plan thanks to computer programming.

speechtext: Like the unemployment insurance plan?

speechtext:
I am coming to that; just be patient. Many citizens envisage arguments and disputes with bureaucrats about their benefits. They see themselves engaged in exchanges of correspondence with officials, appeals to members of parliament and general fuss and bother such as one hon. member just mentioned has gone on in connection with the unemployment insurance plan. We all know there were difficulties with that plan for all concerned, most particularly for the beneficiaries. But it seems to me it should not be beyond our skill to work out a system under which those who qualify for benefits under the new plan will be spared the agony of having to make a case for what is due to them under the law. I really think the minister should assure the House that his officials are, in fact, making all the necessary arrangements and that a computer programming system has been developed which will make the administration of the program as simple and convenient as possible. I am confident that this can be done.
The family income security plan does not come cheaply. It is estimated that it will cost approximately $800 million a year, which is $150 million more than the present expenditure on family and youth allowances. If the government were to retain the existing universal scheme while doubling the amount of the benefits, the cost would rise by an additional $560 million per year. The family income security plan, costing much less, puts more dollars in the places where they are most required. I agree with the minister that it is a more efficient use of the tax dollar.
Opposition spokesmen have been critical of the selective nature of the plan, arguing that the move to selectivity makes it a welfare program, something which universal payments avoided. Do they also argue that selective payments or subsidies to various sections of the agriculture industry are similarly welfare schemes? In northwestern Ontario, where the forest products industry is king, we would dearly love to benefit from something similar to the Prairie Lift program, or from a two-price system for our products. But the need for selectivity has ruled us out. While we do not like it, we realize it is a necessity of life. By the same token, it seems to me that thousands of Canadian families need help, also on a selective basis, in meeting their obligations as parents.
April 20, 1972

This is something that will not only benefit them but help the economy because the money they will spend will be mainly on essential items, thus helping to bring about an acceptable level of family living.
Returning for a moment to that difficult concept of social justice, it seems apparent that justice requires that all shall have the chance to follow the natural human instinct to make for themselves a reasonably happy and satisfactory life. In so far as income redistribution can help achieve that end, governments have a clear and unambiguous obligation to act. To have an equal concern for the good lives of its members requires that society treat people differently, selectively. The unemployed and the sick receive certain benefits. The old receive pensions. Those with families and small incomes receive income supplements, and all of this on a selective basis. The principle of selectivity is fair, it is equitable and it is logical.
I see the family income security plan as an investment, a social investment in families and persons, an investment in which there is almost certain to be a return in human values. If we do not have this plan, or one similar to it, then other and possibly less acceptable means must be found to assist those families with a greater need. Going cap in hand to some agency or another is not the answer, because it humbles our citizens and spawns an attitude of bitterness and resentment.
I see the family income security plan as being an enrichment of the concrete substance of civilized life. If there is to be an enrichment, then it follows almost as an axiom that there must be selectivity. Why fertilize soil that is already rich and producing strong, healthy plants? Some political writers have contended that maintaining a minimum standard of living within a society has less to do with justice and more to do with basic humanity. They have said that the maintenance of minimum standards is a requirement of humanity rather than of justice. All of this is merely semantics. Whether the family income security plan is an example of social justice or whether it is just plain humanity does not matter very much. What does matter, it seems to me, is that this bill receives the support of all hon. members so that it can be passed quickly into law in order to provide financial assistance to so many in this country who are, and will be, dependent upon it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when you read this bill, and it is not a simple bill, you begin to wonder what actually is the basis upon which the government has introduced it. Is it because the young families of this nation have pressured the government to introduce a new measure? Is it because, for economic reasons, they need more money to raise their families? Is it because the government and its provincial counterparts have come to the conclusion that the normal annual increases in these payments are growing at such a rate there is not enough money to go round? Was this bill drafted in an honest effort to give more money to those who need it and less to those who perhaps need it less?
Family Income Security Plan
Was it designed to create actual savings in tax moneys so that less tax dollars would be flowing out? What was the basis for the bill?
When you analyse this bill, Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to find any real basis for the introduction of the measure in its present form. In the present election climate that we are facing, politicians are asking themselves whether this bill was delayed and designed to be one of the last bills in a dying parliament in order to influence voters at election time. Was that the basic reason for the bill?
When you try to answer these questions as honestly and earnestly as you can, you begin to feel that, whatever your doubts, you have sound reasons for those doubts. It seems that during its tenure of office the government has sought to make changes, one after another, to many of our basic laws and basic establishments in the land. Although the reasons for such changes appeared logical at the time, the results under this government's administration, unfortunately for the people of Canada, have in many instances been almost chaotic. Though the government tends to shift the blame for some of its maladministration to the civil service, many of us in this House believe the fault lies in the way these new policies have been introduced. The way they have been drawn up makes it almost impossible to have practical administration.
May I point out some concrete examples of what I mean-and I am not being facetious, Mr. Speaker. I think something is drastically wrong. We changed the basic concept of the postal service in Canada on the premise that we were going to introduce new electronic devices and computers, that we were facing a new age with new methods. Is it not really shameful that we must now face the fact that under this new administration, this new and polished system, it takes as long to send a piece of mail across a street as it took to send it from coast to coast under the old method?
We were told that we were going to have a brand new Unemployment Insurance Commission with a brand new approach to this very complicated subject. We were going to close down all the little local offices and concentrate operations in large computerized centres so that in seconds we could provide a service which perhaps took days before. But what has happened? The story is known nationwide. There has been utter chaos. Instead of reducing the time period within which cheques were issued from days to seconds, in many instances the time has been increased from days to weeks and months.
Then, the government brought in its tax bill, which was introduced as a measure of reform, as a method to simplify tax returns for those who must pay taxes. This bill, it was suggested would make it easier for people to compile the tax they owed the government and would make collection easier. Again, what has happened? The new tax bill is so complicated and complex that even those who produced it say privately and publicly that they do not understand the full ramifications of the measure.

I am wondering about another point. The legislation provides that in order to qualify a person will have to file a statement of his income, and that there may be an exchange of this information between departments. This is serious. Does this mean that if an individual who feels he qualifies for family allowance under the new regulations files his statement of income, this information will be compared with his income tax return filed with the Department of National Revenue? Is this the comparison that will be made? Is this how it will be checked? Will the incomes of the citizens of this country become public property and public knowledge? Do we have to make public all the income and business returns of a family; is this what will happen? This is what the situation appears to be under the terms of this legislation.
I hope the minister will explain some of these things to me in order that I might understand them more fully and in order that the people whom I represent may have an opportunity to understand them. This would be a change in the policy which has existed for a great many years. It is amazing, indeed, when one realizes that over the years many families have used their family allowances for specific purposes, such as the college tuition of the child involved, pension or a trust, special wardrobes or any of the other special expenses which families have to meet. What will happen when this bill is passed? Many families have counted on this money for years and suddenly it will be stopped. What will happen to a family which has been counting on this money to send the children to college? The family has had to live from day to day on earnings, and this little extra every month has been set aside for a specific purpose? What will happen when it is cut off? This is the type of hardship that the cold clauses of a bill often fail to take into consideration.
We who deal with this type of legislation sometimes become so involved in the legal phraseology that we forget the human element. After all, this is the important element and we must consider what we are doing for people. I feel that this legislation will cause an emotional disruption, as has been pointed out by so many people. It will cause an emotional disruption when there are two neighbours on a street who are placed in a different category and who receive different rates of family allowance for children of the same age, when we have people in different regions who, because of the normal economic returns for families, receive far less than people in other regions, or when we have people who have an excess of income one year and who are faced with scarcity the next year. As a result of four months of plenty when they do not need it, they will be registering for the four months of scarcity when they cannot get it. So, we will have hardship after hardship.
Although the principle may be sound, I feel that we will not satisfy the people of Canada because those who will be struck off the rolls of recipients of family allowances will feel that they have been discriminated against and those whose family allowances will be reduced will feel they have been treated as second class citizens. I venture to say that the very few people whom this govern-
Family Income Security Plan
ment is desperately trying to help, those who are in poverty and on welfare, will be directly helped by increases in family allowances. However, they will be just as dissatisfied because they will feel that under the changed plan the family allowances they will receive will not be high enough to improve their standard of living.
These are the reasons I am very much concerned about this legislation. First of all, I do not think we are solving a basic problem. Second, I think we are interfering with an established practice and changing it in such a way as to cause chaos. Third, I feel that we are bringing in just one more piece of legislation, the administration of which will be almost impossible. Fourth, I am definitely of the opinion that if we do pass this legislation we will not satisfy the people of Canada, and we will not satisfy those who will be called upon to pay. This is the group of people whom we sometimes forget. We are certainly humanely concerned with those who do not have enough, but I wonder if we ever stop to think about those people who have enough but on whom every year we impose a greater and greater financial burden. When will this stop?
These people have rights and they are concerned, and justly so. Perhaps they do not need family allowances as desperately as other families but they will feel discriminated against. Certainly, they pay taxes to pay for the present program, and in receiving family allowances they are on the same footing as every other family in Canada, but their level of income makes them subject to greater taxation. They were prepared to accept this program and through the years there has been very little criticism of it, but now they are being told that not only will they be called upon once more to pay for this program but they will be written out of the contract entirely; they will no longer be eligible for family allowances. This is how double taxation is imposed.
There is one other feature of this legislation to which I should like to refer before concluding. Have we not reached a strange state of affairs in the administration of economic justice in this country when we find ourselves ready to reduce the payments for any child in any family to 42 cents a month? This figure has been bandied around because it is the same amount by which the old age pension was increased. When I appealed to my friends to compile as fairly as possible, the cost of administering a 42 cent cheque, I discovered-and I would like to have this checked-that we will be paying $3 in administrative costs every time we send out a 42 cent cheque. This is what the government is trying to tell us will be the Utopia when we are under a computer system and pay people according to their needs. I wonder if anybody will profit under such a measure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on this bill at an earlier stage I likened it to an umbrella that was full of holes, and said we had no choice but to accept it in view of the heavy rain shower that we were suffering. In the

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
interim, I and a number of my colleagues have had a chance to study the measure more closely. Now, I find that the leaky umbrella, full of holes, has collapsed into a mass of metal ribs and torn cloth. It is completely useless to do the job of providing family allowances for people across the country.
Had there been any doubt in my mind about this, I feel sure the debate during the last few days would have removed it. Member after member has brought up points regarding this complicated way of dealing with family allowances, indicating that it is an impossibility, and is an unjust and unworkable measure. As a result, I feel we have no choice at this stage but to abandon the project entirely and introduce a better one in its place. The faults in the bill have been enumerated. I will simply mention them again because they have been thoroughly discussed. The biggest one is the departure from the principle of universality, a principle which was established years ago and which has worked well. What was really required was an increase in the amount of the allowance to bring it more closely into line with today's cost of living.
The second fault is the distortion of the family allowance system from one of ensuring a little more well being for families into one of welfare, to be used exclusively as a social assistance measure.
The third bad feature of the legislation is that it will increase the division of the Canadian people into the have's and have-not's, particularly at a time when it is being borne in upon us at every hand that what we need is much greater cohesion and co-operation among the different sections of our people. At such a time it is most deplorable to divide them still further by such a measure.
The fourth bad feature is the administrative nightmare that the bill will bring about. This is something that has been dealt with thoroughly. When the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) was speaking,
I remembered what one of his colleagues had said earlier in this debate that it had been calculated with respect to measures of this type that only about nine cents out of every dollar reached the people for whom the money was intended. I am not at all enamoured of the way in which computers, armies of bureaucrats, yards and yards of red tape and oceans of paper are supposed to be saving the taxpayers money. I believe that the system of family allowances that we have had, with its universality, is an infinitely better, simpler and fairer method than what is proposed here.
The fifth bad feature of the bill is the costs it will place upon taxpayers who are already over-burdened and who will not share any more in family allowances. One thing we ought to have learned on this continent is that taxpayers do not forgive governments when they are taxed without receiving any share of the benefits. This is exactly what this measure proposes for at least a third of the families in Canada.
The sixth bad feature I would mention, and it is something that has not yet been successfully contradicted, is

that the children of social assistance families will get only half the benefits. I am still waiting for a successful refutation of that statement, and the fact it is so slow in coming indicates there is doubt about the way the bill has been drafted. I will put my faith in my party leader, who is a very competent legal person. He tells us that according to his reading of the measure children in families that are on social assistance will receive only one half of the benefits of the family allowance.
But more than all these things, what brought me to change my mind with regard to the bill was my realization that this is part of a pattern whereby the government is singling out a group of taxpayers, those in the lower middle and lower income brackets, and telling them, "Look, there is only so much money available for family allowances, for old age pensions, or for whatever social measure is under discussion." The government is telling these people, "If you do not want to be crushed into the ground with taxation we must modify the scheme to make sure that instead of universality the money is given to those who need it the most. This is the only way in which you people can be saved from being completely crushed into the ground." It is this pattern, which is completely dishonest and ruinous, that has made me decide that the time has come to make a stand and say we want no more of this deceptive way of slipping things over on the Canadian people. This is the method which the government uses to slip over basically unfair and unjust legislation on the people of the country.
The government tells these over-burdened taxpayers, "We cannot afford to keep this universal system any more. We regret it." As the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) said a little while ago, "We are building the edifice of social justice, and in the process of building, something has to go." What is going is social justice. It is regarded as a crime in Canada to be poor. In the view of many people that is the most evil crime in the country. I repeat that the government tells these over-burdened taxpayers, "We have to limit the family allowance to the people who need it most. We have no more money." Why didn't the government think about that last fall when the tax reform bill was under discussion, when these same lower-middle and lower income groups were saddled with a tax structure which took far more than their share from them, and did not equalize their burden as the incomes of rich people and of corporations rose higher on the scale? Why did this government not say, "We want to readjust our family allowance scheme, to modernize it; we must put in a fair tax system so that those people who are able to pay for family allowance can be taxed when the time comes to make the payments under the scheme." Why did they not do it then?
Let me give some evidence, Mr. Speaker. Recently, a seminar sponsored by the Nuffield Foundation of England under the auspices of the Canadian Council for Social Development, was held in the Laurentians, not far from here. A number of eminent people attended, amongst
April 20, 1972

them Professor S. M. Miller of New York University and Professor Martin Rein of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The latter informed the gathering that if Canadians are ranked according to income, the lowest 40 per cent of the population earned 15 per cent of the country's total income in 1969. The top 40 per cent earned two-thirds of this group. Professor Miller said:
This means that more people are getting rich than are moving out of the most intense level of poverty-this means that those in the lowest group have become relatively worse off, farther below a standard of living which has shifted upwards.
It is these lower levels who are losing out on the rising standard of living in this country, yet they are bearing the burden of the cost of the social welfare schemes.
We are told there is no money for family allowances. But we hear estimates of up to $10 billion for the Mackenzie Valley pipeline and $10 billion for the James Bay hydro and other projects. On Sunday last on CTV the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) forecast that $50 billion will be needed for resource and energy development in Canada over an unspecified period. We know that $1 billion has been spent by DREE since it was founded. There is plenty of money for pipelines and things like that, but no money for people and the needs of people. This is why I believe this bill should be scrapped. We hear talk about the various kinds of evils in government, but I believe there are few evils more insidious and dangerous than those which crusade under the cliches of the just society while pulling the rug from under that group of taxpayers that is hit the hardest. People talk about the increase in the gross national product, but what is the use of that if the GNP continues to be distributed unfairly to the people of this country? That is what is happening now. I cannot get excited about the growth because I know that the more gross national product there is, the more unfair will be the distribution to the people.
The Royal Commission on the Status of Women made a number of suggestions and outlined a number of measures to protect family life in this country. They recommended child care allowances over and above the present system of family allowances. All across Canada, women have been waiting for action to be taken on the recommendations of the commission. The report was tabled around Christmas, 1970. It had 167 recommendations but so far only two of those of any substance have been implemented, both by the minister of labour last session when he brought in legislation under the Unemployment Insurance Act to look after the confinement period of pregnant women, and legislation for the Public Service of Canada which guaranteed that women could have pregnancy leave without injury to seniority and other benefits. These are the only recommendations of substance affecting women that this government has implemented so far.
How long do the women of Canada have to wait for some guarantee or indication of interest on the part of this government? I know all about the task forces that have divided up the recommendations and are studying

them, but I also know that task forces, commissions, boards, white papers, and all the rest are used as a means of putting off the evil day of action. I regret to say that is what appears to be happening in this case. In the Speech from the Throne on February 17, 1972, there appeared this sentence:
Another step and long overdue, consists of policies to ensure the equality of women in Canadian society. These will be announced this session.
The only announcement that this government has made so far this session relative to that sentence is to the effect that one million mothers will be deprived of family allowances and that the children of mothers on social assistance will get only half of the new family allowance. This is a blow and an insult to the mothers of this country and they are not going to overlook it.
Time and again my colleagues in my own and other parties have pointed out what those family allowance cheques have meant to the mothers of this country. Often the lowest income people have had to use the cheque for food, clothing and the necessities of life, while families a little higher up on the income scale have used it for things like school supplies or have put it aside so that the children may have the advantages of higher schooling later on or other things that are deemed necessary. Now, with one stroke of the pen, this family allowance cheque is to be taken from a million mothers on the ground that they are wealthy and do not need it. The government will not get away with this. People will realize, as some of them do already, that it is just plain dishonest presentation and deceptive packaging to say to those mothers "You do not need it and you will have to sacrifice in order to give the lower income families a little bit of a family allowance cheque." They know about the machinery of giving the cheques out and then taking them back again through taxation from those who do not need them. But they won't use this basically fair method.
Just the other day the minister asked me "What is the difference if you give it out and take it all back?" If he only knew about the psychology of women, he would know that often the family allowance cheque is the only money they have to call their own, that they can rely on at all times. It makes a tremendous difference when they know that they can always have that cheque at their disposal instead of having to go to sometimes stingy husbands and ask for an allowance-present company is always excepted, of course. However, there are a great many stingy husbands in this country. Some women have to beg, and they are not going to forget it.
I tell you, this legislation will sharpen people's vision very considerably. They will watch money being poured out like water in the hiring of hordes of public servants who will administer this legislation. They will read the little pamphlets sent out by the government and learn how to keep on the right side of the law, how to avoid being sent to jail if there are fewer children in the family than previously reported, or if certain children become too old for benefits, or if there are changes and improve-

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COPY OF STUDY OF MANPOWER UTILIZATION OF THE MANITOBA GARMENT INDUSTRY
speechtext:
That an Order of the House do issue for a copy of the study by Summerour and Associates Inc., Atlanta, Georgia, undertaken for the Department of Manpower and Immigration regarding the "Analysis of the Manpower Utilization of the Manitoba Garment Industry".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I raise this question for two reasons. First, I think it is important that this material be made public because of the problems which confront the garment industry and, indeed, the whole clothing and textile industry in Canada. These industries have traditionally been and still are to a very large extent labour intensive. There has been very little mechanization in the garment industry. A very high percentage of the cost of producing the garments which are produced and sold in Canada and worn by Canadians goes into the payment of wages for the workers in this industry.
This industry is going through a period of great upheaval. It is buffeted on all sides from the importation of competitive goods from countries which have traditionally paid substantially lower wages than those Canadian workers receive. Countries such as Taiwan, Mainland China, Japan and areas such as Hong Kong, where the wage rates are fantastically lower than in Canada, are in competition with Canadian industry. Therefore, the industry has had difficulty trying to meet the competition of products imported into Canada from those countries.
I am not an expert, but I have been told that one cannot buy a shirt now that retails for less than $10, except for those imported from the countries I have mentioned. This is because the cost of labour in Canada is too high to compete with the cost of shirts produced in those countries to which I referred.
1488

April 20, 1972
Manpower Utilization
In addition to the Canadian garment industry finding it difficult to compete with these countries, it is becoming increasingly difficult, if not impossible, to attract labour into their industry. They must compete with industries in Canada which are not labour intensive, as is the garment industry, but are in fact capital intensive. To give one example, in my own city of Winnipeg, a person who begins work in a packing plant with no experience, training or skill receives a starting wage of substantially more than $3 an hour because these plants are very highly automated and equipment oriented rather than labour oriented. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) is in the chamber. He can confirm what I say. The garment industry finds it difficult to pay more than 25 cents, 35 cents or 50 cents above the minimum wage which, in Manitoba, as in all other provinces, is less than $2 an hour. Therefore, it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to recruit well educated, skilled, trained workers.
I submit that when a study is carried out on manpower needs or manpower utilization of the garment industry in Winnipeg or anywhere else, it is important that the information obtained not be kept secret, locked in the vaults of the government department which commissioned the study. It should be made available to the industry, the unions, and workers concerned and, indeed, all the people of Canada.
I want to spend a few moments talking about the general question of making information available to the people of Canada. As our society becomes more complex, mechanized and automated, governments play a much more active role than in earlier years. It does not matter whether it is the government of Canada, the United States or any other country, nor does it matter which political party happens to form the government. The governments are playing a much more active role than ever before. Canada is no exception.
In this country, we know from government reports and independent sources that the government requirements for information have grown at a fantastic rate. There have been tremendous increases in the number of highly skilled, trained and highly qualified government employees, such as economists and scientists. I am not being critical. I think this is necessary. Maybe we have not done enough of this. They have been given the job of researching many of the basic problems which face the people of this country and with which governments will have to deal. It is not only the civil service which has increased, but to a very large extent many of the problems with which governments have to deal have increased. Various government departments and agents will have to come up with answers in the next one, two or five years. Private groups, companies and individuals, who are supposedly expert in the field, will have to provide information which is required.
There have been commissions, a host of studies, task forces, special reports, or call them what you may, in every field which affects the people of Canada. We have had a task force on social security. We debated that

bill for some time. We have also had task forces on ecology and pollution. There have been studies on scientific research; there have been studies on industrial strategy for Canada. Most of these are, perhaps, required. I am certain that members of parliament who are not cabinet ministers could make worthwhile suggestions to the government concerning other studies which need to be carried out.
The point I am trying to make is really a very simple one. I believe that the overwhelming bulk of the studies which have been commissioned contain information which ought not to remain virtually the private property of the minister or of the department concerned. If the people of Canada are to understand what governments are doing, we must arrange our system in such a way as to provide them with the necessary information upon which to reach valid opinions. Especially is this true as the problems facing our people become more complex.
Let me refer to the debate which has been going on in this House during the last few days, the debate on the family income security plan. I suggest that had members of this House, members of the press gallery and media workers generally as well as members of the public been given access to the white paper on social security prepared under direction of the Deputy Minister of the Department of National Health and Welfare, several desirable consequences would have ensued. All concerned would have been in possession of information conducive to arriving at a consensus about the kind of legislation required to meet the needs of Canada's poorer families and we should not now be conducting a highly partisan debate such as we have heard for the past several days and, no doubt, will be hearing for a number of days yet to come. As it is, members of parliament as well as members of the public generally are not in possession of all the facts involved, facts as researched by a committee under the leadership of the Deputy Minister and incorporated into a report which has since been locked in the files of the government.
I am not suggesting for a moment that there are not some reports which should remain unpublished, for example reports having to do with national security or financial matters, cases where a government is trying to decide whether one company or another is receiving a particular contract. A report of that kind ought not to be made public because the information contained in it might give an unfair advantage to one group or another. But, Mr. Speaker, when we are talking about family allowances or a projected multi-million dollar transportation corridor down the Mackenzie Valley, the people should surely be told all the relevant information. Surely, it is essential that they should be in possession of all the facts. In the case of the Mackenzie Valley project, for example, they should know the estimated cost in dollars, the probable effects upon the ecology, including the damage which would be done to wildlife, the consequences for the indiginous people, and so on. And yet 99 per cent of all these studies conducted in all these various fields are being kept locked in the files of ministers and when hon. members from either side of the
April 20, 1972

House ask for the publication of these reports, they are told this would not be in the public interest because the documents requested are interdepartmental documents. Or some other equally stupid reason is put forward. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talks frequently and eloquently about participatory democracy, about inviting the public to let parliament and the government know how they feel about various issues. I suggest the public cannot really tell the government how it feels about any of these issues unless it has access to the necessary information. And the only way in which the public can get access to these facts is for the government to publish, as a matter of course, the reports and findings of the studies it has commissioned.
I do not question the right of the government to say, apropos of any particular report, that it does not agree with that report or that it accepts only part of it. That is what governments have to do. I am saying that if the government really believes in the kind of participatory democracy about which the Prime Minister has spoken of so often, it should make available to the people in Canada most of the reports on studies which it has commissioned. So, I urge the government to agree to my motion that this particular report having to do with the analysis of the manpower ultization of the Manitoba garment industry be tabled and made available to members of parliament and to the people.
