speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be given a few minutes in which to speak on this subject. After listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) one would be led to believe that he and his hon. friends purposely put down these motions to give them an opportunity to moan and groan and spread doom and gloom on this five o'clock show almost on a daily basis. On many occasions, when we reply from this side, expressing other opinions or making a rebuttal, we are told we are not sticking with the subject of the motion. But, Mr. Speaker, you yourself heard the last speaker bringing the subject of family allowances into his speech, as well as everything else he could think of, and still dragging bottom, not making good sense of what he was saying.
May I tell the hon. members why I am interested in speaking on this matter? It is because the garment industry in Manitoba, where I come from, traces its origin to the Winnipeg Shirt and Overall Company established many years ago in 1899. I shall make a few remarks about its history, but I assure you I intend to return to the question on the production of papers in a few moments. The industry provides about 40 per cent of the manufacturing employment in downtown Winnipeg. Its early history was one of producing work clothes, primarily for the prairie market, in small facilities scattered across Winnipeg. The success of these firms depended on the personalities of the owners-the Freeds, Stalls, Steinbergs, Jacobs, Berkowitz and others -who were instrumental in establishing the foundations of the industry in the province.
Today, many men continue in the traditions of their fathers, with new personalities extending the fashion
Manpower Utilization
industry into its current dimensions. There are some 200 firms and production includes children's wear, coats, headwear, sportswear, rainwear, pants, blouses, gloves, leather apparel, suits, sweaters, uniforms and skirts, to mention a few. A significant export market has been developed in the United States and Europe and its value of exports per employee is believed to be higher than that of the industry elsewhere in Canada. I should like to return to this point in a moment. The industry early centralized in the warehouse district of downtown Winnipeg, where approximately 90 per cent of the firms are still located today, and where most employees prefer to work. Many of these are from my constituency.
I said a while ago that exports are very important to this industry. On January 22, 1971, as reported at page 2685 of Hansard, I had this to say:
The shipments to date ol these 126 companies amount to $79.1 million, and the companies employ 6,300 workers... I think these figures prove the point I have endeavoured to make.
In light of these figures, it is fair to say that the Canadian clothing industry is one of demonstrated capability. It is in fact competitive with clothing industries of other developed countries from the point of view of style, quality and price.
In fact, to prove this I went on to quote an article that appeared in Maclean's magazine for June, 1970 praising the style and quality of Canadian made garments. The article was entitled "You mean all that stuff is Canadian!" and I pointed out that it was an article that all Canadians should read. It describes what articles Canadiens are making, exporting and wearing. An article also appeared in Men's Wear magazine in October, 1969 and I should like to quote it again because it is important:
Merchants say the reasons for more imports from Canada are rising prices of the European market, better deliveries, cooperative manufacturers and good quality and fashion ... we like English fabrics, but the cost was getting too high. Now, we get the same fabrics from Canada... at a much lower price-
Two stores in the Atlanta area carry Canadian merchandise: Rich's and Rogue Specialty Shop. Rich's clothing is store labelled and purchased through the AMC buying group. The Rogue carries a line of leather goods and suits from Canada. Gerry Underwood, Rogue owner, reports the suits are one of his most advanced lines and bring a premium price-
The merchandise manager for another major men's wear outlet spoke well of a Montreal clothing resource which supplied suits for his firm under a private label.
The reason I quote that again is to let the House know the capabilities of this industry in Winnipeg, and I quite agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North said about it.
In addition to this clothing industry we have a textile industry in this area. There are two firms. One of them is the only textile women's hosiery plant west of Toronto, located in my province at Tevlon, in the Interlake region north of Winnipeg. The company employs 85 people. There is also a fabric knitting textile plant located in Selkirk which knits the only yard material and is the only plant west of Toronto. It employs 110 people.
The report made by the consulting firm of Summerour and Associates is one of which many of us would like to know the outcome. At the same time, other studies have been made so I think we can say that the industry knows

speechtext:
These recommendations were aimed at developing management and personnel policies that would improve working conditions, stabilize employment, and improve productivity.
In the last few years the industry has responded well. Productivity has been greatly increased, which has contributed to the improved material welfare of the workers. Further, their job contentment has increased through such things as improved working accommodation and staff relations of all kinds. Our local officers are now enthusiastic about the industry as a source of employment and an officer from headquarters, with considerable knowledge of this industry, recently visited Winnipeg and confirmed our local officers' reports.
It will be seen that this study was in reality an assessment of conditions and needs within an industry. Such assessments are continually being made by our officers to enable us to make the best possible allocation of manpower funds in the face of our numerous demands. In this instance, the operation was more complex than usual because the problem was a complex one, but it was essentially an operational undertaking and the results are expressed in what are essentially operational departmental papers. This is not a consultant's report in the usual sense; you do not get one oh a major industry for $7,000. The consultants simply provided the framework within which the study should be made and assisted in the analysis of data.
However, the department conducts many such studies without consulting assistance. All require the full and free co-operation of employers and workers in the industries involved and none could be conducted if it was

thought for a moment that the word of manpower and immigration officers could not be accepted. More than this, we could close the doors of every Canada Manpower Centre, for neither employer nor worker would have confidence in us.
The simple fact is that many employers of an important industry and a provincial government department undertook a joint effort with a federal department on the word of its officers that any findings would not be made public unless all consented. That is the crux of the matter. The provincial government is involved. First, I believe we should have the permission of the province before these findings are released. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) knows this. This is the reason I made the comments I did today. He knows this as well as I do. The industry in the province has specifically declined to ask for this consent.
I should like to mention that many items have been introduced in the textile industry magazine. In fact, I have prepared these comments from that magazine and would like to say a few words on it. The year 1971 was an eventful year for Canada's textile manufacturing industry. In fact, it might well go down in history as a year in which more solid progress was made in several directions than at any other time in the past decade. The federal government has recognized that the industry is well managed, efficiently operated, has a remarkable degree of flexibility and indeed is important to the national economy. Proof of this lies in the fact that in 1970 the government announced its national textile policy and set up the Textile and Clothing Board. Actually, this board commenced functioning in November 1970, before Bill C-215 to establish it was passed into law last May.
Establishment of a national textile policy has been advocated by industry for some time and when this became a reality, industry, through the Canadian Textile Institute moved into high gear to provide full co-operation to the federal government through its Textile and Clothing Board agency in an all-out effort to right the many serious wrongs with which industry has been afflicted for so long. In addition, and in accordance with the policy terms of reference, industry set about putting its own house in order. Restructuring programs have been undertaken and it is safe to say that as a result of a much closer working arrangement between government and industry vis-a-vis adoption of a textile policy and the setting up of the Textile and Clothing Board to study and recommend government action, the over-all position of industry is gradually improving.
Certain it is that the T and CB has been exceptionally active throughout the past year or so, with five reviews conducted. This activity has been and continues to be matched by the CTI with the provision of voluminous briefs and other pertinent data essential for presentation at board hearings. And, while hearings will continue, it is encouraging to note that T and CB rulings on completed hearings have not been countermanded by government and have been, by and large, encouraging to industry. I am not saying these things; it is the people of
April 20, 1972

the textile industry who have said this in their own magazine.
I continue my compilation of the comments in the magazine. Year-end statements by senior executives appear to bear out this assumption. As one executive put it:
The textile industry for the first time in several years is giving every indication of being able to build from a firm base. This is largely the consequence of the government's implementation of a national textile policy which has assured industry of a continuing reasonable share of the domestic market-
And again:
Canadians have been through some difficult economic time and have developed both a flexibility and a ruggedness... and there is, perhaps, a wider acknowledgement that greater employment will depend largely on encouraging the increase of our own manufacturing industry-Reflection of this in the textile industry has been the adoption of a federal textile policy with the textile and Clothing Board to study and recomend government action where needed to sustain efficient Canadian enterprises... Application of such recommendations in keeping with national goals is the key to halting the loss of jobs and retaining a reasonable share of the market for Canadian mills-
There are other slightly less positive statements, but in perspective the views expressed weigh heavily in favour of what has been done in concert between government and industry and will continue to be done to preserve the textile manufacturing industry as a thoroughly viable operation well able to make a generous contribution to the improvement of Canadian manufacturing as a whole. Mr. Speaker, during the past hour a number of hon. members have evinced considerable interest in the garment industry in Manitoba. They are to be commended for this interest. It is an important industry so far as Canada is concerned. It is not only important to Manitoba, but to all of Canada.
Since its inception, the Department of Manpower and Immigration has concerned itself with the critical shortage of staff which has been characteristic of the garment industry in Manitoba. Understandably, the department has made special efforts, both through immigration and training in industry, to attempt to meet the employment demands of the industry in Manitoba. Between April 1,

April 20, 1972
Manpower Utilization
1967, and June 1, 1969, the cost of such special measures approached $300,000.
In 1969-this matter has been covered by previous speakers-the department felt that additional efforts were warranted. In that year the department invited the industry and the Manitoba department of industry and commerce to join with it in a study to determine the extent and causes of the labour turnover. It was the view of the government that the relatively high labour turnover and the chronic labour shortage should be made the subject of a probe, so a committee was formed representing the two levels of government and the industry. Co-operation was extended not only by the previous provincial government of Manitoba but by the present provincial government. That committee was known as the clothing committee.
The garment industry itself arranged for some 20 firms to participate in the study, with their officers, and over 200 present and former employees agreed to be interviewed in depth. They were given an assurance that anything they said-and some of it, I must be frank with the House, approached the defamatory stage-would be held in absolute confidence. Those were the terms and conditions. Surely this is the source of the difference which appears to exist between the mover of the motion and the government. I choose to believe that the mover of the motion does not fully understand the background or he might have hesitated to bring forward the motion.
With that guarantee, the workers and employers provided full, frank and in some cases subjective opinions on matters of staff training and working conditions. Most of the interviewing was carried out by officers of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The firm of Summerour and Associates, highly experienced in the field, was retained to provide technical advice on the structure of the study. It was a condition of the contract that all results would be confidential to the clothing committee and its corporate members. This position is still supported by the government of the province of Manitoba, which acted in good faith. That government should be commended for its willingness to carry out a commitment given to the working people of the province by a previous government.
A number of recommendations were made to enable the industry to reduce turnover through improved training and personnel policies and many firms are reported to have implemented them. Indicators show that as a result of these improvements in the Manitoba clothing industry, its outlook is excellent. I can tell the House that it is anticipated that shipments will rise to $110 million by 1976 and the number of employees will increase very greatly. Not only is this important for Manitoba and the working people of that province, but it is important for Canada as a whole because the Manitoba clothing industry, the firms making it up and the skills of the workers of Manitoba are providing Canada with major foreign earnings today. They are not doing it because they enjoy any natural advantage over some other parts of the country; they are doing it through entrepreneurial skill, the skill of the workers, imagination and design ability.

The formation of the clothing committee and the job that was undertaken, the co-operation between two levels of government, the industry and the working people, must go down as a successful enterprise which is bringing great results in terms of higher wages for the working people of Manitoba and greater benefits for all of Canada. I want hon. members to be assured that if the House were to approve this motion it would result in the government breaching a contractual agreement with a provincial government and a major Canadian industry. This we refuse to do. It would violate a promise to the workers who participated in the study and might well cause some of them embarrassment. We refuse to do this disservice to the working people of Manitoba. It would destroy the usefulness of an effective economic tool that could conceivably be used to improve the lot of other Canadian workers in the future.
This was a successful technique initiated by the federal government through the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Because of the nature of the study, the type of information sought and received and the commitment made to participants, neither the industrial nor the provincial representatives on the clothing committee will agree to the publication of this report. We concur in this stand. We stand with the other members of this tripartite arrangement, the clothing committee, and we do not believe that approval should be given to this motion which would result in the government breaching a contractual agreement with a provincial government and a major Canadian industry. April 20, 1972

ing with the tremendous bureaucracy that the new legislation would organize, create and control throughout Canada, as it happened with the Canada Pension Plan, which we accepted in principle, while being against its terms of application. We maintain that Bill C-170 will create a bureaucracy that will be very costly to the Canadian taxpayer.
As an example, I have just mentioned the Canada Pension Plan. In today's edition of the Montreal newspaper, La Presse, one can read the following:
Administration costs of the pension plan have tripled.
That is not what we were told when the bill was introduced in the House, but today we And that the plan's administration costs have tripled the paper adds:
Administration costs of the Canada Pension Plan have more than tripled in the last six years increasing from $6,003,805 to $21,153,238.

-But to come to that, administration costs had to be tripled. I quote further:
As of last December 31, 91,524 pensioners were receiving a monthly pension of less than $20 under the plan.
Mr. Speaker, such administration cost to pay out pensions of less than $20 to the majority of pensioners are high indeed.
There is more to quote:
The amount contributed to the plan, including the interest and other income resulting' from the investment of contributions, reached a total of $1,076 million in 1971.
And with that amount of $1,076 million in 1971, we paid pensions of less than $20 to almost a majority of the pensioners under that plan. The government keeps on saying it was generous because it paid out so many millions of dollars but they are not distributed among the Canadian citizens receiving a pension.
This is why, in m|y opinion, Bill C-170 constitutes discrimination towards the majority of Canadians.
The bill under study deals, as its title indicates, with payments to be made in respect of children-i.e., to those who have children in their custody. Clause I really defines the whole purpose of the bill-it reads as follows:
Family Income Security Plan.
Clause 2 contains the definitions. This is an important clause, because you constantly have to refer to it as you study the bill. For instance, the base calendar year, as regards family income, is the basis for granting allowances applied for.
Clause 2(2) defines the income of a person for a calendar year-which is his income computed in accordance with the provisions of the Income Tax Act, minus any death benefit paid to him under a pension plan.
It is to be noted that, under this bill, family income is calculated by adding together the incomes of both parents-the father's and the mother's-on which the formulation of the new family allowance proposals is based.
Family Income Security Plan
Payments are made from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for any child under 18 years of age in the custody of a citizen residing in Canada. However, if a province makes payment to youths between 16 and 18 years of age, as is the practice in the province of Quebec, no payment is made to children from 16 to 18 years of age by the government of Canada if the latter grants tax abatements in this connection to the said province. This is pure and simple discrimination towards a province- in this case, Quebec-and no account whatsoever is taken of the decisions or positions of provincial authorities.
Clause 6 of the bill is without question the most important and the most complex. It is perhaps more complex than important. Monthly benefits of $15 in respect of children under 12 and of $20 for children from 12 to 18 will be paid.
As indicated in paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of subclause 1 of clause 6, a ceiling has been placed on family incomes so that when this ceiling is reached or exceeded, allowances in respect of children decrease and sometimes disappear according to income or to the number of children.
Mr. Speaker, since the bill now before us is unjust and unacceptable, my colleagues of the Social Credit party will support the amendment moved by the New Democratic party in favour of the universality of family allowances.
We do not want to take away from the haves to give to the have nots. That would be unadultered socialism or communism. This is evident in the USSR, in Czechoslovakia and other socialist countries. This does not surprise us at all from a Canadian Prime Minister with a socialist and even communist bend!

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I wondered whether the member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) might be one of those on the secret list of 20. At any rate, 1 assure him I definitely dissociate myself from the remarks of the leader of the Social Credit party: I think it is obvious that we do not share his philosophy regarding that particular incident.
The bill before us deals with the family income security plan to replace the Family Allowances Act which has been in effect since 1945. The leader of our party, when speaking to the House yesterday, said that our party finds the bill completely unacceptable. I share that point of view for a number of reasons, but primarily for two basic reasons which I think will come back to haunt the government. First, the question of universality has been discontinued in this bill and replaced by the principle of selectivity. Second, it will become a bureaucratic nightmare which I believe will make the crisis we had in respect of unemployment insurance during the past winter look like child's play when we begin dealing with all the regulations under the bill.
I would also like to make it clear that our party believes we should have in this country substantially increased basic family allowance rates. Our party has made that clear from the beginning. However, this is not the reason we are opposing the bill on second reading and have moved an amendment. Our party wants this bill to be universal rather than selective which I believe is a bad principle which pits neighbour against neighbour, friend against friend and indeed family against family in certain communities. Our party also believes that if we are to have equity in this country's social programs, there must be drastic changes to the Income Tax Act and our taxation laws.
The family allowances program was first introduced in this country on July 1, 1945. At that time I believe 35-1972-4*
Family Income Security Plan
the government made a number of assumptions which basically were very good but which they are abandoning in Bill C-170. First of all, they gave recognition to the fact that families with children have special needs in our society. They recognized the fact that when a family has children it has needs which are basically different, special and extra to those of people who do not have children.
Secondly, under the legislation enacted in 1945 the government recognized that to ensure a greater measure of equality of opportunity for all children, such a measure was needed. These are two principles that I believe are being thrown out of the window either in total or in part under Bill C-170. The program as originally introduced in 1945 was not a welfare program; it was not a poverty program: it was money set aside to assist the mothers of Canada to raise their children and to provide them with some of the basic necessities of life. This is the principle that is being abandoned in the plan before us. It is becoming part of a welfare plan, and when you have selectivity such as this you attach to it a stigma that divides people.
As I have said, the need for such a plan in 1945 was to make up for some of the deficiencies in our system and our way of life. We wanted to provide something extra for families with children because I think everybody realized that when a person gets a job, whether he be a labourer, a teacher or a farmer, he is not paid according to the size of his family but according to his ability or the special status of the job. The family allowances program was one of the many ways in which we hoped to overcome this type of inequity in our society.
The old legislation recognized the importance of children to our country and the fact that they have special rights. It stipulated that the expenditure of the money from this fund should be used to help our children. I come from a family which was by no means affluent. My family was relatively poor, and I knew as a child growing up that the family allowance was of great assistance to my mother.
This principle will be lost in the new Family Income Security Plan, and it is a principle that should not be lost. Under the old Family Allowances Act the payment for children under the age of six was $5, for children aged six to nine it was $6, for children 10 to 12 it was $7, and for children aged 13 to 15 it was $8. In 1957 these payments were adjusted upward. In 1964 we introduced in the House a youth allowance for those aged 16 and 17. We now find that many of these principles which existed in the old family allowance plan are no longer part of the plan which is before us.
The new plan is not universal; universality has gone out of the window and we have adopted the principle of selectivity. The new plan is very much like the guaranteed income supplement for our senior citizens. They receive a basic $80 a month and if they are really poor they may receive a supplement of about $57.70 a month. There is a graduated scale under which if you

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
make a small amount of money the guaranteed income supplement is reduced.
I know, from travelling in my constituency which contains thousands of old age pensioners, that this is one of the complaints about which I hear perhaps most often except for farm problems. I refer to the frustrations which people have with this type of system, with the means test-frustrations which they have vis-a-vis their own families and others in the community. Despite this plan we know that hundreds of thousands of old people in this country are living in poverty, in conditions of which members of this House should be ashamed. We know, also, that this type of plan under the Old Age Security Act has created a needless amount of bureaucracy. It means the disclosure of a person's income. It creates a stigma. It causes a means test. These are matters which I do not think the Canadian people appreciate.
The new plan introduced in Bill C-170 is based primarily on three things. First, and most important, it is based upon the income of the family. Second, it is based upon the number of children in a family, and third it is based upon the age of the children. The amounts to be paid out under the bill are $15 for children under the age of 12 and $20 for children between the ages of 12 and 17. We And in the regulations that a family with one child, with an income of $4,500 a year, will not benefit from the plan. In other words a family with one child, earning less than $4,500, will qualify for the maximum payment. For each additional child the family income is allowed to escalate by $500.
According to the Minister of National Healtn and Welfare (Mr. Munro), the number of families who will benefit to the maximum will be fewer than one million. We find that for each $100 of additional income, the monthly benefit will decrease by 33 cents. If you add all these figures together you get the following result: 25 per cent of the Canadian families will be better off under the new plan than they were under the old one. We know that even this was questioned in the House the other day.
We find that some of the people under the plan will qualify for only one-half of the benefits. We know also that some of the provinces in this country might see this program as a means of paying less welfare as welfare amounts are adjusted and set according to family income. So perhaps not all the people who qualify on paper for the allowance will actually be better off a year or two from now.
We find that under the new plan, 42 per cent of the people will receive partial payments; they will not receive the maximum. Of this 42 per cent, about half will receive less than they are receiving now, and half will receive more than under the present legislation. We find that roughly one-third of Canadian families, or 33 per cent of one million mothers, will not receive any assistance under this legislation. I think that many of this 33 per cent are not very well off.
Many people will not receive any assistance at all are in the income bracket of $5,000 to $10,000 a year, and you certainly cannot consider them to be wealthy. Many of

them are farm people in our constituencies. They are working people, unionized people, and some professionals such as teachers. Indeed, many of these people are average Canadian citizens. They will be subsidizing those who will receive benefits under this plan. In the long run it will create a great deal of misunderstanding in our society when one group of people who are not making very much have to subsidize those who are making slightly less. This is a way of turning one group in our society against another. It will divide our society and build up resentment. I will give one or two examples of what I mean. Let us consider a family, with one child, living in Toronto or Ottawa and making $5,001 a year. Under this plan they will not receive any benefits. Such a family is not, by any stretch of the imagination, wealthy. This situation will develop resentment in our country.
We find that a family with two children, both under the age of ten, with an income of $9,000 will receive a monthly payment of $3.60, which is less than they are receiving now. And the poor themselves, as I was saying earlier, do not get a much better deal. They are given a few crumbs, a bit of tokenism, a little bit more money, but that is all. A family with four children all under age ten, earning less than $6,000, will get $1,720 a year in payments, but under our archaic income tax laws such a family will lose $400. That is some deal for the people of Canada who need help!
The answer to the question before us today is obvious. We need a plan that first of all is universal. We need a plan that does not have a means test. We need a plan that has a higher basic rate of payment. And we need a fair taxation system. If we do not get these things and this bill goes through without amendment, then the new plan will create more resentment in communities and families than we have now.
I want to say a word about a subject dealt with eloquently this afternoon by my colleague from Van-couver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). It concerns the fact that under this bill many women feel they are discriminated against. Here I am thinking of hundreds of thousands of women who will no longer be receiving family allowance cheques. This is a point the government should keep in mind. It should not be too surprised if it finds that by next fall many of these women are very angry. The second major concern I have about the bill is that it will become an administrative, bureaucratic nightmare. I said earlier that it will make the unemployment insurance crisis look like child's play. The costs of administration will skyrocket. We already know, from an answer given by the government, that the present staff of 730 will have to be doubled to 1,477 as a result of this bill.
The new plan will cause a great deal of confusion in the minds of applicants. It will create a lot more paperwork for bureaucrats, a lot of needless expense that not only frustrates people but turns them against governments and government plans, including many of the better plans which we have in this country. It will create among people hostility to a family allowance plan that
April 20, 1972

could be good if we followed a few of the basic principles and philosophies advocated by many citizens.
Now I want to spend a few minutes considering some of the bureaucratic hang-ups and difficulties that we can get into with a plan of this sort. All applications for family allowance must be checked to determine the eligibility of the applicants. This is obvious under the type of regulations we have. We could get away from many of these difficulties if we had a universal program for all families according to the number of children in the family. Secondly, in the case of eligible applicants payment is based on family income and the age of the children. One gets into a great deal of paperwork if the family income changes and as the ages of the children change.
In the case of non-eligible applicants, appeals and explanations must be handled. We will have people applying who do not qualify. This will cause more bureaucratic hang-up than is necessary. Abuses of the plan must be handled. We all remember the unemployment insurance program and the Lift program with which western members in particular are familiar. You cause a great deal of resentment among people through the appeal procedure. Cases involving a substantial increase or decrease in income must be processed, with appropriate adjustments made to benefits. There may be an overpayment for some reason, or an underpayment. Again, adjustments must be made, causing great difficulty.
What about divorces and the effect they will have on the regulations? We have separations; we have marriages. These must be reported if the family income is affected and the benefits must be adjusted. When you have marriages, separations and divorces-and there are tens of thousands of them every year-it throws more bugs into the plan. Adjustments must also be made to benefits when estimated income differs substantially from actual income. We may find that some people halfway through the year will take a second job, driving a taxi or doing night work. The wife may start teaching in high school or in the local elementary school. As a result, the family income will increase.
Administrative machinery must be set up to recover payments made to ineligible persons. Here again, western members know the difficulties we had with Lift when the administration tried to recover overpayments that had been made. Expert administrative machinery must be set up to detect frauds such as misrepresentation of income, misrepresentation of the ages of children, misrepresentations as to the number of children, failure to report income and failure to report deaths, marriages and separations. This is the type of bureaucratic jungle that we will get into with this bill. Finally, administrative machinery for liaison with the provinces will have to be established. The courts will probably be burdened with new offences and people who are guilty will be liable to fines and, in some cases, jail terms.
These are some of the problems that our party is concerned about. We could avoid many of these unnecessary bureaucratic hang-ups if we had a plan that was universal, that made payments regardless of income, and if
Family Income Security Plan
we had a fair taxation system that did not allow payments to be made to the very wealthy. The position of our party is supported by the Social Development Council. I wish to quote briefly from a brief presented by that council:
Family allowances should be universal, paid to all families with dependent children as a social right thus avoiding divisiveness among families and any element of stigma. The present program has this feature but FISP would eliminate it.
This is precisely what we are trying to get across to the minister.
There should be the maximum feasible simplicity and efficiency in administration. These features are virtues of the present family allowances program but FISP would undoubtedly be considerably more complicated and costly to administer.
The program should be as fully compatible as possible with long-term social and fiscal policies. This is not evident in the FISP proposals.
The program should have a built in escalation clause to meet the full amount of annual rises in the cost of living. This feature is not included in either the present program or FISP.
These are some of the things the Social Development Council is concerned about and that our party is concerned about. These are some of the reasons we are trying to get the government to make important changes in the legislation. As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, basically we want three things. We want payments to be larger, we want them to be universal and we want the tax system to be reformed so that it is equitable and just. To me it seems very contradictory that we have so much money in this country for unnecessary things but when it comes to dealing with the average citizen we do not have enough money. I become very angry when I see some of the large tax loopholes that are available to the very wealthy and to large resource companies. During the last ten years, on average the gas and oil companies paid taxes on only 5.7 per cent of their profits.
What do we have for the poor people, the average worker, the farmer and the small businessman in our country? Basically, we have nothing but a government program that is so bureaucratic, so complicated that it will alienate half the people and do nothing for the other half.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the family income security plan one could become really concerned or look at it light-heartedly and say that perhaps it is a step in the right direction and all will be well once it is established. I think this question touches upon some of the deep-rooted philosophies that must be engendered, endured and borne by those in government. It touches upon the question of whether to be a pragmatist in government, operating on a day to day basis, solving the crisis of today tomorrow and the crisis of tomorrow the day after. But, Mr. Speaker, I think we have in Canada used this type of approach too long in government and it is time we decided upon our goals.
I have been involved in politics for 14 years, and when I compare society in Canada today with what it

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
was when I became involved I realize that the country has changed a great deal. Fourteen years ago I was a young man coming to Ottawa.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: You are still pretty young.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Thank you. Fourteen years ago I had a fixed concept of what made Canada tick and what made me proud of it. I was proud because I looked upon Canada as a society of middle income people with a low proportion of people who might be termed the exalted rich or the desperately poor.
An hon. member suggests that I might be blind, I wonder how old he was 14 years ago, and how well he had travelled Canada. I recognize him as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight). I think he was elected at 24 years of age, so 14 years ago he would have been ten years old, and probably had not travelled far from the town of Weyburn, Saskatchewan, and had no real information as to what made Canada tick.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: And still does not.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Nor had he any idea of what classes there were in our society.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Just the middle class.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I was proud to be a Canadian in those days. We managed our economy and our society better than the United States, better than Great Britain, and we did not get into all the problems of Europe, East and West Germany, and so on. As Canadians, we had a lot to be proud of. As I measure success in the management of our society and the economy, I can only reach the conclusion that the situation has deteriorated.
We have seen a tremendous increase in the number of exalted rich, a tremendous increase in those who feel they should be classified as the desperately poor, and a shrinking of the middle-class society. The people in the middle class must carry the load in our society and pay taxes to support the desperately poor. They must also carry the load so that the exalted rich may escape paying taxes. Some hon. members may wonder how this can be, but there is a great machine called regional economic expansion which will hand out money to anybody and give all kinds of credit and relief in the form of grants. Many of the wealthy international and foreign companies located in Canada pay very little taxes bemuse of the grants they receive. Indeed, sometimes the grants far exceed the amount they pay in income tax. We hand it back to them saying it is their duty to provide the jobs we desperately need-so much money for so many jobs. This is the criteria and concept we are involved in. I think it is time we paused to examine the cause of the problem, Mr. Speaker. It is partly due to the fact we have developed schemes which undermine the hard working wage earner, the person in the middle class category.
According to Statistics Canada, the average wage is in the area of $135 a week, roughly $7,000 a year. This

is about the middle category. Under this new program, 30 per cent of the people now receiving family allowance will not receive it any longer; the next 18 per cent will receive less,' the next 17 per cent will receive about the same amount and the next 35 per cent will receive more. The $7,000 a year wage earner will find himself in the position of asking whether he should try to earn more and declare his earnings, only to receive less because the universality of the family allowance program has been removed.
I have philosophized, Mr. Speaker, in order to indicate why I think this program is leading us in the wrong direction. I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), is this the only program on the statute books? I think I read in the Toronto Star that the minister said it is unrealistic to think that we can support present welfare and health care costs. Those may not be his exact words but he said something like that.
What does this program do, Mr. Speaker? It destroys the universality of the family allowance program. The old age pension is universal. I ask the minister if this is next to go. He shakes his head in a negative manner; I want that to appear in Hansard. I wish the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) were in the House to shake his head in a negative manner too. We would be so much wiser and so would the minister. The old age pension and the hospitalization programs are universal. Anyone who is a citizen receives provincial hospitalization coverage. The millionaire can enjoy medicare as much as the desperately poor.
Then we introduced unemployment insurance. It doesn't matter how great your assets might be as an individual. You might, if you wanted to, sell your business or your farm and put $2 million in the bank and go to work for an average kind of income. After working for 180 days you might quit and collect unemployment insurance. A man might have even $3 million in the bank or $3 million worth of stocks and bonds: he would still collect unemployment insurance if he had paid into the fund. There is a universal concept in the unemployment insurance program.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Do not forget medicare.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I mentioned medicare, hospitalization, the old age pension and unemployment insurance. There may be other areas I could deal with but they do not come to mind. Is the government's action in approaching this program on a selective basis the beginning of an attempt to destroy the universal application of a number of programs which have been passed and which reflect some degree of credit on this House? One might ask why I, a Conservative, am speaking this way, why I am concerned about universality. If you destroy the concept of universality, you will cut off from benefit not only the exalted rich but the people in the middle. Today, most people in Canada are in the middle. At least, it can be said that most were in the middle a few years ago: I do not think most people are in the middle today.
April 20, 1972

At the top end of the scale are the exalted rich and then you come to where most middle-class people were, or are. Those people will be asking themselves this question: "Shall I duck a little? Shall I quit working this month and perhaps not earn too much? Shall I moonlight a bit so that my apparent income will stay the same? After all, I will get free hospitalization and medicare benefits and I will qualify for the old age pension next year when I retire. Is it worth while working so hard?"
Do you see what I am getting at, Mr. Speaker? Destroying the universality of these programs will eventually erode the will of some Canadians. I think hon. members know what I am getting at and where my argument is leading. Most Canadians frown on the suggestion that people really do not want to work. For example, why cannot I hire a man? Why must I work 16 hours a day at a filling station in Calgary or wherever it may be, simply because I cannot hire a man to operate the pumps? After all, it is not a hard job; all he has to do is put the hose into the tank of a car.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Perhaps that is why the hon. member is never in Ottawa.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) says that is why I am never in Ottawa. I want to make it clear that I do not own a filling station. I was saying that merely to illustrate my point. If the hon. member thinks I am never in Ottawa, let him consider this: why have many Liberals been coming to Crowfoot and saying, "That terrible member for Crowfoot is a thorn in our sides. He holds up legislation," and does this and that. How can one who is never in Ottawa do that, I ask?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
I return to my argument. Many people running small businesses find it difficult to hire people. Why, Mr. Speaker? I say our society is turning industrious, serious and conscientious people off. It is destroying their incentive to work. Let me give another example involving income tax. Some say, "If you earn extra money you will go up into the next bracket and they will hit you with a 40 per cent rate." People do not want that. A hired man who has worked for me for many years said, "Can I earn more money now without increasing my taxable income?" I said, "Yes, you can earn more money and more of your income will be exempt from tax because of your increased exemptions. However, the money you earn will be taxed as a higher rate and you will pay a higher rate as a bachelor once you start making substantial amounts of money." He said "I will have to watch that." There you have a prime example of how a seriously minded person can be turned off, so to speak. Similarly, the proposed family allowances program which is to be part of our social security legislation will have a tendency to turn people off.
I am reminded of a poem I read a long time ago entitled, "Lifters and Leaners". The author is un-
Family Income Security Plan
known. What it says is true of the direction in which our society is going today. The poem is as follows: There are two kinds of people on earth today,
Just two kinds of people, no more I say.
Not the saint and the sinner, for 'tis well understood,
The good are half bad, and the bad are half good.
Not the rich and the poor, for to count a man's wealth,
You must first know the state of his conscience and health Not the happy and sad, for the swift flying years,
Brings each man his laughter and also his tears;
No, the two kinds of people on earth that I mean,
Are the people who lift, and the people who lean.
I fear that is the direction in which Canadian society is going. We are dividing Canada, not into a society of the exalted rich, the middle-class and the desperately poor but into those who lift and those who lean. This piece of legislation will penalize those who are lifting and encourage growth in the number of leaners.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: There are those who lift and those who lean.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Yes, that is what I said.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Those are the two kinds of people on earth.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: The poem reads, "There are two kinds of people on earth today... the people who lift and the people who lean." I think that is true.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: And there are those who refuse to lift or lean.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at one time we had an industrious middle class in Canada, willing to work and earn and contribute to Canadian society. We had a few exalted rich and a few desperately poor, yet most were in the middle. Today the middle-class is shrinking. In other words, there is a different sort of division in our society today. Government have encouraged growth in the number of those willing to lean. An increasing number of people say, "To heck with lifting." I was going to use a stronger adjective but thought better of it. People are fed up with contributing to a society that does not appreciate them and overtaxes them. Basically, this bill will tax them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: The hon. member is selling Canadians pretty short.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
The hon. member, who is rarely seen here and who seldom speaks in the House, says I am selling Canadians short. I want Canadians to be strong. I want to be vigorous. I want them to buck right in there and hit the collar, as we say in western Canada. As legislators, we are not encouraging them to do that. I am not saying all people are fed up with working. I am not saying all people are not prepared to do their bit. I am saying that we as legislators are encouraging many of them not to work. We are encouraging many to become leaners. This whole concept is wrong.
One of the greatest evils in our society today-I say this without hesitation-is the politician in this House

April 20, 1972
Family Income Security Plan
who can swallow himself whole on a day to day basis. There are too many persons of that kind in this House. They hope that at the end of next week or next month, through some great undercurrent they will again rise to the top, float and be able to say "1 was okay. Nothing really hurt me. That is what the folks wanted and that is what we gave them. They do not know it will hurt them in six months." This is the kind of politician I despise. If all the people in their constituencies wanted candy tomorrow, they would give it to them. However, they will not be back here after the election this fall.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: It is the 14-year politician who does that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: I have often wondered about the age of the Prime Minister. I did not know whether he was 14 or 16. It seemed to me it had something to do with even numbers. I did not know whether he was 16, 18, 36, 38, 46, 48 or 52. I knew his age was on even number.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: You forgot the opening remarks of your speech.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: I never forgot them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: You thought Canada was great 14 years ago.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: I thought Canada was great 14 years ago, and I still think there is potential for Canadian greatness. However, we as politicians must recognize our evil and wayward ways.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Quit selling us short.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: We must correct the situation and quit being guided on a day to day basis by politicians who believe they can swallow themselves today. They give the people what they want today and hope it will not catch up with them tomorrow.

I see the Minister of National Health and Welfare has returned to the chamber. I wish to direct a question to him.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker; I will do my best but the House seems to be in a mood to heckle. Normally I am not distracted by idle remarks made by members to my left and members opposite, but it appears that I was bothered this evening. I apologize to Your Honour and hon. members for allowing myself to be bothered.
I wish to direct a simple question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I hope that before this legislation is passed the minister will explain the statement I read in the Toronto Star yesterday, that it was unbelievable or unrealistic to expect that Canadians can stand the welfare or health costs of today and then bring forward a piece of legislation which will increase the basic cost from $640 million a year to $800 million for the coming year. We all know that after a few years these costs build up and proliferate. How does the minister explain that concept? Is this the kind of system that will repay itself, such as the old age security pension plan? No, it is not. It is a direct drain upon the taxpayer. The exalted rich escape paying taxes and the desperately poor are not in a position to pay them. This is an increase in tax for the shrinking middle-class. That is my first question.
Second, in destroying the universality of the family income security plan or, as it is commonly called, the family allowances plan, is this the first step toward destroying the universality of many other social justice programs?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Socialistic?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: I said social justice. You treat it any way you like. It means different things to different people. To us it means fair play for Canadians. To the Liberals it means fair play for the Liberals.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Excuse me, Your Honour; I am being sidetracked again. Is this the beginning of destroying the universality of the hospitalization program, the medicare system and the unemployment insurance system, which does not come under this minister's department? Before I was interrupted by the catcalls I had referred to the old age security program. While I do not place much credence in the minister's remarks, because we know the Prime Minister rules all his ministers, with the upcoming election the minister's remarks should be on the record. Under the new cabinet system of evolving policy, the Prime Minister rules everything, the cabinet and a couple of other important people. Some people have referred to them as the three wise men, and the minister is not one of them.
April 20, 1972

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: I am not one of them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Even though the minister may be overruled by the inner cabinet, to use a polite expression, with the upcoming election he should place his views on record. As the leader of the Liberal party in Manitoba asked about another piece of legislation, is this the tip of the iceberg? I ask this question with regard to the concept of universality in social justice programs that has been long established in this House and the Canadian system. If it is, it amounts to a re-enaction of the means test. The means test draws a line down the middle, and this is where we find the man who carries the lunch-pail, the man who is earning $135 a week. In effect, we are telling him, "Duck below the line and you will get certain services provided free by the government. Do not stick your head above that line, whatever you do." That is the curse of a means test. A means test may be all right in the case of persons over 70, but is the House aware that 67.4 per cent of those over 70 are living below the poverty level? I do not think it is. Yet this is a fact attested to by Statistics Canada.
Are we taking a retrograde step today? Are we returning to an all-inclusive means test which will affect every worker? I have told hon. members what this proposal means. It means that 30 per cent will get no benefits, that 18 per cent will get less, that 17 per cent will get the same, and 35 per cent will get more. Seventeen and 35 make 52. We are right on the halfway line. A person earning less than $7,000 is wise to continue to earn less than $7,000. A person earning more than $7,000 is wise to get below that figure somehow or other. Don't work for two months; go moonlighting where the people in the inland revenue cannot catch up to you. The minister smiles. If he only knew how many people are doing that in today's society. If he only knew how many teachers, how many farmers, how many lawyers-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Lawyers?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Doctors?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Yes, lawyers. I said that because the Minister of National Health and Welfare has a law degree. I heard the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) throw in the word "doctors". Yes, doctors, teachers, dentists-you name it! We are all human.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: And ranchers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
And ranchers and farmers. We are all human. Draw the line. Recreate the cruel means test. It will apply to the working person and you have caught the guy who carries the lunch-pail, who goes to work every day. Is there not some reward for him in this society? I was about to use a bunch of adjectives such as the average working man would use, but I thought better of it. This will strike at the man who carries the lunch-pail, who eats baloney sandwiches or peanut butter sandwiches, or whatever it is, every day and goes back home for a hot dinner at night. If a man earns more than $10,000 he will get nothing at all. And his wife will
Family Income Security Plan
say, "What are you doing with my money? Give me some money. You are taking the pin money; you are taking the cream cheque money, the egg money." My mother used to get the cream cheque; we boys milked the cows.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Don't forget the cookie jar, Jack.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: The cookie jar was always empty; I had a sweet tooth. But this is removing the money which the average wage earner's housewife really felt was hers. She spent it on the children. She bought little Susie a new dress. She bought little Peter a new pair of shoes.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Or a Barbie doll.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Or a Barbie doll. She bought milk for the children or maybe she got a hairdo one week out of 17. There was no need to ask her husband for the money; it was her money and she spent it on the family.
The average housewife will be right on the line. Is her husband earning more than $7,000? If he is, she gets less. If he is earning more than $10,000, she gets nothing. Ten thousand dollars is not a lot of money today in the cities, although it is a lot of money to the farmers and to many other people. Thank the Lord, as far as the farmer is concerned it is net income, it is taxable income and it may therefore not affect very many farmers. But it will affect a great many housewives in the cities. We are told that by 1980 two-thirds of the Canadian people will be living in our major population centres.
Then there is the likelihood of inflation. I do not wish to go into the subject very deeply, but with an increase of more than 30 per cent in the money supply experienced this year, and a 21 per cent increase last year, by next fall, when this legislation really hits home, inflation will be running wild. The Liberals say, "We hope the election will be over by then, and everything will be great." But a year from now, with wages increasing in line with the rate of inflation allowed by the government, the $7,000 limit will not suffice and an increasing number of average wage earners will be disqualified from benefit under this measure. So the average housewife will have less money to spend on her family, the family she treasures, the family she tries to encourage and raise.
For these reasons, I believe the legislation to be a retrograde step and I support the amendment now before the House. I hope, should the amendment be defeated, that a worthy colleague of mine wiM move an amendment warranting the support of the most vocal heckler I have encountered this evening and, also, the support of the triumvirate sitting in the front row of the NDP benches. I sometimes wonder which one is the leader, but they all make a fair stab at it and I would like to think that they would support a further amendment.

speechtext:
Maybe there is not too much left to say, but I will say this, Mr. Speaker. For those on the other side of the House, for those who are the government tonight, there is a great deal left

to say. Before this bill is dead, buried and forgotten they are going to hear it said. I suggest to those on the other side of the House that they think a little more and remember why and under what circumstances this legislation was placed on the statute books of Canada. It was placed there by a man who for a number of years was one of the most consummate politicians to grace the scene, Mackenzie King. He brought in the legislation at an appropriate time, as well as bringing in certain other legislation. He did so, not because he was a progressive reformer but because he was a politician and the CCF party was breathing down his neck.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext: Who are they?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE BENEFITS IN RESPECT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
If the people to my right do not remember who they were, we will refresh their memories during the next election campaign. And that goes for hon. members opposite too. The legislation we are talking about tonight was brought in for these reasons. Let us give the man who at that time was head of the Liberal party credit that he was enough of an economist to understand that we have to find ways and means of distributing income to those who are disadvantaged. I do not think he would have brought the legislation in except for that, and for the fact he was being threatened by members of the CCF who were offering the Canadian people an alternative to poverty and hardship and the Canadian people were beginning to believe them.
Therefore the family allowance legislation was brought in, as was unemployment insurance. These were two basic programs that were introduced, both of which are now being sabotaged by this government led by a technocrat with ice water in his veins, a man with no basic concept of what this country is all about, who cannot bring to bear an understanding of how to use the wealth we produce. Since he and his party cannot conceive how to use the wealth of this country, they must bring in programs that share poverty around. The options are either to use the wealth that society can produce or to ensure the existence of the privileged few who sit at the top, while sharing the balance of the poverty around.
Look what has been done to the unemployment insurance legislation. Members on the back benches as well as on the front benches-though the latter have some expert help available to them-are trying to solve the problems that the unemployment insurance bill has created in an endeavour to relieve the misery visited on those who cannot quite conform to the new circumstances.
The government is now going to turn the family allowance legislation around and we shall be doing the same thing again-trying to correct the injustices, inequities and unworkable situations that will be created. Can the government tell me how it is going to administer an act that bases the right of an individual to claim payments on the income that he declares, when his income may vary anywhere from $3,000 to $8,000 from one year to the nexit? Certainly this will be the case with fishermen, farmers, people in urban areas where the wife may work for five months of the year, or for 12 months, or not at all if she is bringing a child into the family.

How in the world will the government even things out? The previous speaker mentioned that you will be pretty well able to tell a person's level of income by seeing whether he claims a family allowance cheque or not.
What baffles me is why we need this legislation in the first place. It would be far simpler to use the taxation system and tax back surplus income in the higher income levels. But instead of that, the government are increasing the amount of family allowance cheques. They are devising a way to get their fingers on an individual to whom they think they are giving some money, but secretly think that they and their family do not deserve it at all. Their real wish would be to take the money away entirely, but they cannot quite get away with that and know it, so they have to fiddle around and half clobber it. That is the objective of those on that side of the House; that is what they are after.
Led by a technocrat, advised by people in high finance who if they had to run their own business would have been broke yesterday, the government is continuing its folly. Hopefully, before this debate is concluded the government will recant, change its mind and back away from this folly that they now propose to visit upon the Canadian people.
May I call it ten o'clock?

OIL-INQUIRY AS TO REVOKING OF DRILLING PERMITS FOR BRITISH COLUMBIA COASTAL WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, March 8 as recorded at page 635 ol Hansard, and on Tuesday, March 14 as recorded at page 798 ol Hansard, I asked certain questions ol the Minister ol Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) seeking to ascertain whether or not the government had issued oil drilling permits to Petrotar Development Limited ol Calgary covering 2.7 million acres ol coastal waters ol British Columbia. The answers to those questions were so inconclusive and evasive that I decided to put this matter up lor debate on an adjournment motion.
I want to point out that the revelation that these permits had been granted came in the British Columbia legislature Irom a statement made by resources minister Ray Williston which accused the government ol Canada ol talking out ol both sides ol its mouth by agreeing to any exploration in Queen Charlotte sound while publicly agonizing about offshore oil pollution.
When these lacts came to light, the hon. member lor Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) immediately rushed to the press to assure the public that no such permits would be issued lor exploration ol offshore areas with-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
out the approval ol the Minister ol the Environment (Mr. Davis). According to the Fisherman ol February 9, the Minister ol the Environment himsell described the lederal permits as an error which would not be repeated. On February 4 he was reported as saying that he had discussed this politically sensitive issue with the Minister ol Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister ol the Environment is quoted as saying he was assured there would be action to recover the permits.
Consequently, I have been trying to find out, first, whether these permits were issued and, second, whether or not they have been rescinded. I therelore placed a question on the order paper, question No. 322 ol March 16 ol this year. It was passed as an order lor return yesterday, April 19. Here are the questions:
1.	How many oil exploration permits were issued by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources during 1971 covering areas of the coastal waters on the Pacific coast?
This is the answer:
1.	40 oil and gas exploration permits.
The second question is as lollows:
2.	How many oil exploration permits on the Pacific coast were outstanding as of March 1, 1972?
The answer is:
2.	237 oil and gas exploration permits.
I will skip question No. 3 and come back to it later. Question No. 4:
4. What permits, if any, have been revoked since January 1, 1972?
The answer is that there were none. Question No. 3 reads:
3.	What were the names and addresses of the companies granted these permits, on what dates were they issued and what is the area and the location covered by each permit?
The lollowing is the answer:
3.	A list of the oustanding permits, their dates of issue and area covered by each permit is attached as Schedule A, together with a permit map.
A list of the companies holding these permits and their addresses is attached as schedule B.
I have that map. It is rather interesting that the oil permits granted cover practically all of the west coast of Vancouver Island and practically all of the coast of the mainland with the exception of the Strait of Georgia. For from the statement which was attributed to the Minister of the Environment that these 40 permits granted to Petrotar Development Limited of Calgary would be rescinded, we find that they are still in existence, that they have not been revoked.
The Minister of the Environment himself seems to have had a change of heart. I have here a copy of the speech which he delivered on Monday, March 13 to the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union in Vancouver. In that speech he said:
The likelihood of serious damage occurring of course varies from place to place. Out on the big bank off Tofino, we don't have the same urgent problem as we would have were the same spill to occur off Satuma for example.

April 20, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
It is interesting, with the Pacific Rim Park located in that area, and with Long Beach in that area, that the minister did not think it is a sensitive area. He went on to say in the same speech:
Let me make my own position quite clear. I am opposed to the drilling tor oil in Georgia Strait. But I am not opposed to drilling for oil everywhere on our big continental shelf. I am not opposed to it 400 miles out on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. I am not opposed to it 40 miles west of Victoria either.
The minister may not be opposed to it, but the people in my constituency are opposed to it because this would bring drilling down to areas such as Port Renfrew, Jordan River, Sooke and Metchosin. Not many people in that area are aware of the fact that a present there are five drilling permits granted in the Strait of Juan de Fuca, covering 161,450 acres. We want a clear statement from the government as its policy. Who is going to grant these permits? Is the Minister of the Environment going to have the final say, or are we going to get the same sort of thing we had in 1968 and that we have had again this winter, of one minister granting permits and another saying they will be revoked, but the permits stay and the drilling continues and the coastal waters of B.C. can be polluted by oil spills?

With the concurrence of my minister, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) announced in Vancouver on March 13 that exploration and drilling for oil would be excluded from sensitive offshore zones. Our departments will work together on the definition of these offshore zones. The total west coast acreage is 16,272,694 acres, covered by 239 permits outstanding. If any of Petrotar's permits should fall within environmentally sensitive zones, then we will be discussing with that company the kinds and conditions of work which will not be allowed. I should like to confirm the government's position that subject to this zoning, exploration and drilling will be encouraged in the offshore frontier in strict adherence to regulations currently enforced by my department and judged to be among the most stringent anywhere in the world.

Permit acreage may revert to the Crown by reason of surrender of a permit or half permit by the permittee, cancellation of a permit by the minister, expiration of a permit, surrender of a portion-50 per cent or more- of the acreage within a permit area upon conversion of the permit acreage to lease form. NATIONAL DEFENCE-RENT INCREASES FOR MARRIED QUARTERS-SUGGESTED DELAY UNTIL PARITY WITH PUBLIC SERVICE ACHIEVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my presence here this evening arises from questions that I asked on St. Patrick's day, March 17, recorded at page 919 of Hansard. These were in connection with the attitude of the government with respect to its decision on rental rates for married quarters at Canadian Armed Forces bases.
On that date I put essentially two propositions to the minister. First, I asked whether or not it was right that the government's decision, to change the basis on which the rents are assessed for married quarters, was based on the decision to proceed to parity, so-called, between the Canadian Armed Forces and parallel positions in the public service and, if that in fact were true, whether the government would not admit that it would take at least a full year before this came about. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) replied:
Mr. Speaker, it is an interesting suggestion. I think, however, that the hon. member is quite correct that the eradication of inequalities is done in two stages and will not be completed until next year.
I then asked, if it is in fact based on parity, would the government not consider delaying implementation for a full year. The new rental systems, while relieving to some degree the rents being paid by about 7,000 or 8,000 families, impose in some cases substantially higher rents on about 16,000 or 17,000 families. If the principle of eradication of the inequalities between the Canadian Armed Forces and parallel positions in the public service is a valid one, why is it that the government will not even give consideration to this particular request?
Secondly, when will the government get around to recognizing the difference in relationships between veterans, Canadian Armed Forces personnel who served during war and personnel who have not had that opportunity, because of their age and the accident of their particular period in the Canadian Armed Forces, who are not qualified veterans in the sense that they are eligible for reasonable percentage rates, if you will, or funds for the purpose of buying a home, building a home, and major rennovations to existing properties? And will the government now give some consideration to a major review, not only of the rental situation that exists with respect to Canadian Armed Forces married quarters but of the whole way in which we treat present day serving members of the Canadian Armed Forces?
I made a suggestion in the question I put to the President of the Treasury Board on that day. The question appears at page 919 of Hansard as follows:
I wonder whether he would initiate discussions within the cabinet with respect to a system which would permit Canadian forces personnel who are compelled to a major degree to live in rented quarters during their careers-
April 20, 1972

Mr. Speaker, an opportunity to build equity would be a method by which a percentage of their rent could be set aside against their retirement so that they would have the funds with which to establish themselves more readily in the civilian community. These are two reasonable requests. They have some urgency and the government has an obligation to its armed forces personnel to be aware of their social needs and the difficulties they face on retirement. They should be aware, as well, of the difficulties faced by young families with growing children which have the usual commitments of most families today.
I have not seen the minister for a couple of months and I wonder whether he comes to the House of Commons any more, but perhaps whoever is to speak on his behalf could give us some thoughts on these two or three points which are minor in a way though major in consequence to Canadian armed forces personnel.
