maintopic: POLLUTION-WRECKING OF FREIGHTER "VANLENE" NEAR PACIFIC RIM PARK-STEPS TO SUPPLY ADEQUATE EQUIPMENT FOR CLEAN-UPS AND STRENGTHEN NAVIGATIONAL RULES
POLLUTION-WRECKING OF FREIGHTER "VANLENE" NEAR PACIFIC RIM PARK-STEPS TO SUPPLY ADEQUATE EQUIPMENT FOR CLEAN-UPS AND STRENGTHEN NAVIGATIONAL RULES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the first occasion on which I could secure the floor during the question period following the visit to the ill-fated Vanlene which grounded on a rock near Pacific Rim Park off the west coast of Vancouver island, I raised a question which I hoped to address to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) with regard to what steps were to be taken to prevent similar, blundering types of disaster in the future. I suggested that it was more by good luck than good management that we avoided a major ecological disaster.
In particular, I wanted to know what had been done under regulations coming under the new part XIX of the Canada Shipping Act. I also raised some questions about improving methods of clean-up. I intend to raise the question of the shipping regulations tonight. I think it is much more important to consider prevention than to attempt to arrive at a cure after a disaster has happened. In this connection, may I refresh the memory of the House with regard to what part XIX of the Canada Shipping Act provides. Section 739(1) of the Canada Shipping Act provides that the governor in council may make regulations among other things:
(g)	requiring ships in waters to which this part applies and with respect to which the regulations are made applicable to have on board, maintain and use appropriate charts, tide tables, lists of lights and other nautical publications;
(h)	respecting the number and qualifications of navigation and engine room personnel, including pilots and lookouts, required to be on duty on ships of any class designated in the regulations in any waters to which this part applies and with respect to which such regulations are made applicable;
(i)	prescribing procedures and practices to be followed by persons on board ships in order to ensure safe navigation in waters to which this part applies; ...
(o) establishing compulsory traffic routes and other shipping traffic controls considered necessary for safe navigation in waters to which this part applies and with respect to which those regulations are made applicable;
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, those regulations were not effected in this case. I suggest to the House that even if they had been effected, they would have been ineffective to the extent that the act up to now has applied

April 20, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
only to Canadian waters, that is, within the 12-mile zones and within the fishing zones of Canada. I wish to draw to the attention of the House the fact that just over one year ago, on March 1, 1971, I moved a report stage amendment to that legislation which would have provided that the act would apply to waters outside our fishing zones and territorial zones to a distance of 100 nautical miles seaward.
I am glad to see that some hon. members of the House have become interested in the subject since the recent disaster. I wish the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Groos) and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) had seen fit to support my effort to have that kind of additional safeguard written into the legislation at the time it was being considered by the House. If those additional provisions had been in effect, and if the regulations had been in force, obviously the Van-lene could not have run into the rock off Austin Island. Imagining he was still eight or ten hours steaming distance from the nearest land, the master, according to preliminary news reports, thought he was in a position that was somewhere opposite the shore of the state of Washington.
I suggest it is not much use our going through the long and painful exercise, as we do in the House and committee, in enacting legislation if that legislation is merely to gather dust on the shelves around Parliament Hill. Rather, these regulations ought to have been in effect. The kinds of controls that are suggested in the legislation should have made this particular shipwreck unnecessary and should have prevented it. It is one that could easily have been avoided if the regulations, in conjunction with the provisions of the Pilotage Act which we also passed in the previous session, had been in effect.
May I point out that the Pilotage Act provides that the pilotage authority may, with the approval of the governor in council, establish compulsory pilotage areas and prescribe the ships or classes of ships that are subject to compulsory pilotage. In the interpretation section, the act reads:
(d)	"compulsory pilotage" means, in respect of a ship, the requirement that the ship be under the conduct of a licensed pilot or the holder of a pilotage certificate;
(e)	"compulsory pilotage area" means an area of water in which ships are subject to compulsory pilotage;
While I am very happy about the fact that the Van-lene did not cause any major ecological disaster despite the fact that the long-term damage of the oil that did escape has not been fully assessed, nevertheless if it had been carrying a cargo of oil instead of a cargo of motor cars manufactured in Japan bound for the port of Vancouver, we could have had a disaster on the west
coast of Vancouver Island equal to or greater than the one that occurred in Chedabueto Bay some time ago.
In raising this question I hope I will get an affirmative answer from the government that the regulations under the two acts to which I have referred will become effective immediately and a full assessment will be made of the inadequacies that have been revealed in the clean-up efforts which took place in connection with the Vanlene wreck.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
maintopic: POLLUTION-WRECKING OF FREIGHTER "VANLENE" NEAR PACIFIC RIM PARK-STEPS TO SUPPLY ADEQUATE EQUIPMENT FOR CLEAN-UPS AND STRENGTHEN NAVIGATIONAL RULES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, limited as I am in my time, I cannot reply in a precise way to the hon. member, certainly not in the manner that I would wish. I think the hon. member from Comox-Al-berni (Mr. Barnett) will find that he has the full support of all members of this House in the desire to see the greatest possible degree of marine safety employed in Canadian coastal waters.
I understand that the hon. member and my colleague from Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) visited the wreckage site of the Vanlene and saw first-hand the work being administered by federal authorities in an attempt to minimize the pollution threat from that vessel. I am informed that a great deal of progress has been achieved in setting up our national contingency plans for this type of pollution, and that millions of dollars are being spent to provide the necessary tools to cope with major oil spills. The Department of Transport has an extensive equipment program under way. Contracts have been let for the construction of specialized equipment and other types of anti-pollution devices are being procured.
Hon. members may recall the success of the Great Lakes contingency planning structures with the U.S. authorities. That plan went into effect last summer. There now are similar plans for the east and west coasts which will provide for joint response and support in areas which are of mutual concern to our country and the United States.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) indicated to the House on Tuesday, April 18, the progress which is being achieved with respect to the enactment of regulations under part XIX of the Canada Shipping Act. These include oil pollution prevention regulations, ships' garbage regulations and traffic routing regulations. In the final stages of planning are additional regulations which will affect ships' navigational appliances, charts, publications and deck watch. The shipping industry has, of course, been consulted on these matters and it is anticipated that they will be gazetted in the next three or four months.
